Mr. C. E. BOTHWELL (Swift Current) presented the fourth report of the special committee on electoral matters, as follows:
Your committee was instructed by order of reference dated March 13, 1939, to study and report on "Methods used to effect a redistribution of electoral districts in Canada and in other countries, and to make suggestions to the house in connection therewith," but regrets that it has been unable to give this order of reference the consideration it merits, owing to the number of meetings necessarily devoted to consideration of suggested amendments to the Dominion Elections Act, 1938, the last of which meetings was held on the second instant.
Your committee gave consideration to the methods in use in Great Britain, Australia, New Zealand, the Union of South Africa and in the United States, together with suggestions made by the counsel as to how redistribution could be effected in Canada.
Your committee, however, concluded that there are many important questions, including that of the relation of urban to rural population, as it may be affected by the next decennial census, that should receive detailed study before a definite decision is made.
Your committee therefore submits, without further comment, a statement of the methods employed in other countries, and the suggestions made, for the consideration of the house.
All of which is respectfully submitted.

Mr. A. L. BEALTBIEN (Provencher) presented the fourth and final report of the select committee on radio broadcasting, as follows:
The select committee appointed to consider the annual report of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and to review the policies and aims of the corporation and its regulations, revenues, expenditures and development, begs leave to present the following as its fourth and final report.
1.	Your committee was impressed by the increasing scope and importance to Canada of the corporation's work. It feels that more

Radio Broadcasting
effective steps should be taken, through broadcasting itself and other appropriate methods of disseminating information, to familiarize the public with its varied activities.
2.	Your committee is satisfied that the financial policies of the corporation are sound. The corporation has consistently achieved a prudent surplus. Your committee believes that increased revenue should result from improved coverage and service.
3.	Your committee notes with satisfaction the development of the plan of national coverage especially in the prairie and maritime provinces, where 50,000 watt regional transmitters are being added to the national network. In the further development of the plan, the committee approves in particular of the corporations intention to proceed at an early date with much needed improvements in coverage and service in southwestern Ontario and British Columbia.
4.	In regard to programs, Canada is in the happv position of having at her disposal a wide variety of material both from outside and -inside the country. The corporation's policy and practice appear to take advantage of this situation, while giving the maximum encouragement to Canadian talent. The plans for the king's visit are noted with approval. The committee especially endorses the corporation's proposals for a larger number of programs for rural listeners. It is felt that broadcasting can be an imoortant agency of practical service to farmers, fishermen and other primary producers, and of bringing the riches of music, drama and other forms of entertainment and culture into their homes. Your committee also feels that the corporation can do much to instil an appreciation of the value and advantages of the rural way of life.
5.	Recognizing the necessity of planning and balance in public service broadcasting, your committee notes with approval the corporation's determination that the present ratio of commercial to sustaining network programs should not be increased.
6.	The committee of last year emphasized the importance of establishing, at as early a date as possible, a high power short wave broadcasting station, financed as a national undertaking, but operated and controlled by the corporation as an integral part of its system. Such a project would facilitate the exchange of programs with otlier countries, would serve to advertise and interpret Canada abroad, and supplement the domestic program service.
Canada is the only leading trading nation without such facilities. We desire to draw the attention of the government to the imminent possibility that further delay in proceeding with the undertaking may result in Canada losing altogether the short wave channels registered in her name, and as a consequence, being shut out of the field entirely.
7.	Your committee approves, as in the widest interests of the nation, the corporation s policies regarding short wave, television and facsimile broadcasting. The corporation hopes shortly to occupy the field of high power short wave transmission. As regards television and facsimile, the policy is to alienate no part of the public domain to private interests. The corporation intends, as soon as possible, to undertake experiments in facsimile broadcasting.
8.	Your committee recognizes that the responsibility of controlling and coordinating all broadcasting in the public interest rests upon
the corporation. In this connection your committee wishes to express its gratification of a better understanding between private stations and the corporation, recently attained.
9.	Your committee is seized of the difficulties of working out the principles of freedom of speech in relation to the peculiar characteristics inherent in the medium of broadcasting. In view of the limitations, both of time and of the number of channels available for broadcasting, as well as the exigencies of program planning, your committee is convinced that fairness in the presentation of controversial material can best be assured by means of any system of network broadcasting on a sustaining
10.	Your committee shares the view of the corporation that network broadcasting of programs of opinion on current affairs should not be available for commercial sponsorship, more adequate time to be provided for commercial sponsorship, more adequate time to be provided free for this purpose. The committee believes that the corporation's policies respecting broadcasts of opinion are designed to ensure the largest possible measure of fairness and equality of opportunity. We wish to emphasize the importance of placing before listeners the widest variety of points of view. It is desired to stress the importance of flexibility and experiment in forms of presentation.
11.	Certain of the corporation's policies affecting the public generally have not been sufficiently made known resulting in misunderstanding and inconvenience. Your committee approves of the corporation's intention to make such policies known more fully and widely in the future. While recognizing the rapidly changing and developing character of the enterprise, the committee wishes to stress the need of duly publicizing policy decisions of this kind.
12.	On the matter of prfitical network broadcasting, your committee is of the opinion that serious consideration be given to placing such broadcasting during federal and provincial election campaigns, on a sustaining basis exclusively, with the understanding that the time so provided will be divided equitably among the political parties. Your committee is also of the opinion that network party political broadcasting between elections should remain open to purchase, subject always to consideration of fair distribution and program planning.
13.	Your committee recommends that the licence fee for privately owned broadcasting stations be revised in relation to power and population served, and that the new scale be effective for the current fiscal year.
14.	Your committee believes that the existing regulation which imposes on the vendor of a radio set the obligation, before making a sale, of ascertaining that the purchaser possesses a licence, should be rescinded. It recommends that the vendors of receiving sets be in future required to report monthly to the Department of Transport the names and addresses of all purchasers of sets, including the date of each sale. [DOT]
15.	Your committee wishes to record its warm appreciation of the public spirited manner in which the board of governors and the management are discharging their duties as trustees of the national interest in broadcasting. The corporation is developing a broadcasting system of increasing service to the people of Canada.
A copy of the minutes of proceedings and evidence is annexed hereto.
All of which is respectfully submitted.

subtopic: MOTION FOR SITTING ON SATURDAY, MAY 13

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MOTION FOR SITTING ON SATURDAY, MAY 13
speechtext:
That on Saturday, May 13, 1939, this house shall sit from 11 o'clock a.m., and that the order of business and procedure will be the same on Saturday as on Thursday.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, it has been customary as we approach the end of a session for the government to ask the house to sit on Saturdays as well as to have morning sittings. May I say at once that the purpose of the two motions which appear in my name, one to have the house sit on Saturday of this week, and the other to have the house sit in the mornings, beginning tomorrow, until the end of the session, is not in order so to hasten the business of the session that we may prorogue when his majesty is in the city. I have come to the conclusion that with the amount of business that still remains on the order paper it would be difficult for the house, without undue haste, to conclude its business in time for prorogation on Friday of next week. The purpose of the motions, however, is so to advance the business which remains to be done before their majesties arrive in Ottawa as to justify a short adjournment at that time and to render unnecessary a long adjournment over the entire period that their majesties may be in Canada. I believe it is the general wish that such adjournment as may be necessary should if possible be short rather than long.
As I announced some time ago it was the intention of the government that when the house adjourned on Friday of this week it should remain adjourned until June 19 by which time their majesties would have completed their visit to Canada. I still hold the view that for many reasons that might have been a preferable procedure, but I doubt very much if it accords with the wishes of the great majority of hon. members of the house. On the other hand, I do feel that there is a desire on the part of hon. members to bring the business of the house to a close as rapidly as it can be done without impairing in any way what may be necessary in the

3816	COMMONS
Business oj the House-Saturday Sitting
way of discussion. If we sit on Saturday and one or two days next week it should be possible for the house to conclude its business within a very few days after the time fixed for adjournment during their majesties' stay in the capital. The intention, therefore, is not to adjourn on Friday night until June 19, but to have the house sit on Saturday- we are not asking the house to sit in the evening just in the forenoon and afternoon as we did on Saturday last-and then to sit on Monday and Tuesday and adjourn to the time fixed for the royal assent on the following Friday. After the royal assent, it is intended to adjourn again until the following Monday. This means that there will be an adjournment over the time their majesties will be in the capital, but not any longer. I think with that arrangement, considering the progress made during the past few weeks, the house will be near enough to the end of its business to permit of prorogation very shortly thereafter.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MOTION FOR SITTING ON SATURDAY, MAY 13
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must confess that the government change their mind so often that one does not know from day to day exactly what a proposal is going to be when it gets before the house. When we discussed this matter some time ago I said that I thought it would be impossible to get through the business of the house in time to have prorogation by His Majesty the King. I am glad the government recognizes this, according to the statement to-day by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). I said that our party desired to cooperate in every way, because this is an historic occasion; but I pointed out before, and I repeat now, that the business of the house should be attended to without improper haste and without lack of care for the public interest. I should like to point out that the responsibility for the length of the sittings and for proposals of this kind must naturally be the government's. After all the Prime Minister is the leader of the house. It is he and his government that bring in the legislation and estimates and arrange for the appointment of committees. They are in full control of the whole business of the house. This is particularly so to-day when the government has such a large majority, roughly three times the number of the different opposition groups.
I think the government are largely to blame for the fact that we cannot complete our business in time to have the king conduct the ceremony of prorogation.

speechtext:
I am going to deal with the reasons in a moment. The fact is that the important legislation has come down weeks too late. In the speech from the throne, the Prime Minister had his excellency refer to certain legislation that was to be brought down, but exactly two and one half months later, on March 27, the Prime Minister brought down a list of legislation twice as long as the list that had been suggested in the speech from the throne. Most of that legislation was not of any importance, but the most important bills were left too late in the session. Probably the most important bills to be considered this session are those of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) dealing with the western prairie regions. The bill with reference to the marketing of farm products other than wheat was dealt with only last Thursday although it was introduced long ago. The wheat cooperative marketing bill was dealt with last Thursday. The prairie farm assistance bill, referred to as the bonus for the western prairies, was not dealt with until Friday. The bill of the Minister of Trade and Commerce dealing with an initial payment of 60 cents a bushel on wheat has not been touched at all except in general discussion. None of these measures was dealt with until Thursday or Friday of last week. On top of all that, the government has made very many changes in this farm legislation as brought down. First there was to be a dropping of the wheat board and selling by futures. Then a change was made and we were going to have a wheat board and an initial payment of 60 cents. That was all changed and now the payment is to be 70 cents; and after the slating which the exMinister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) gave the Minister of Trade and Commerce last night-and I would advise him to look it up in Hansard-I would imagine that the advisory committee he recommended will be the next change to be accepted by the government.
Another very important piece of legislation, not brought down until the dying days of the session, was brought down only last Saturday, three days ago, by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning)-his bill to establish a central mortgage bank. To my mind this is a most important and intricate piece of legislation, involving government debentures amounting to $200,000,000. Even in these days, when we deal in astronomical figures of finance, $200,000,000 is not picayune by any means. While this bill, as I pointed out briefly the other day, in a few remarks lasting five minutes, deals

Business oj the House-Saturday Sitting
to some extent with financial institutions that lend money in this country, it does not cover borrowing and lending between individuals, as the Minister of Finance himself admitted; and he admitted also the importance of my suggestion in that regard. I want to make clear that I am not opposing the principle of this bill, but it is so extraordinarily important that I believe it should go to the banking and commerce committee. In these dying days of the session-because they are literally the dying days-a bill of such importance should not be introduced into the house at all. While I am not opposing the principle of the bill, I repeat, it must go to the banking and commerce committee, in my opinion, if it is to be properly dealt with. There the financial corporations, and individuals as well, would have the opportunity to be heard. I have already received protests from financial institutions against the legislation and protests as well from individuals. I do not know what the Minister of Finance has received, but I understand-I speak subject to correction- that a great deal of lending is done in Quebec, not by financial companies but by individuals to individuals. I do not know whether that is so or not, but that is what I was told by a lawyer from the province of Quebec, and if that is true, there is no relief provided by the bill for the people of the province of Quebec.

Then there is a huge amount of estimates to be voted, including defence. There has been great talk about the defence estimates, and certainly they will require full discussion. I want to facilitate the business of the house, and so does this party, and I am agreeable, as I think this party is, to the motions as they are at present-there has been a change made by the Prime Minister-to sit in the mornings. I would have objected to sitting in the evening on Saturday, but the Prime Minister says he is not going to suggest that now, although that is how the motion reads. As to next week, I think the majority of our members would be perfectly willing to sit in the mornings on Monday and Tuesday, but there is a great deal of opposition from my followers to sitting on Saturday at all. I do not know how the house generally feels. We are quite willing to abide by the decision of the majority, although we would object to sitting on Saturday evening. If we are to sit at all on Saturday we should not sit on Saturday night, no matter what else we do.
In view of the discussion that is going on throughout this country-perhaps some of it is not very responsible, but there is a body of opinion expressed in conversations to the effect that we are hurrying the business of parliament merely to prorogue. Therefore I think it is very important that we should see that business is carried on in an orderly manner in the interests of Canada.
Before sitting down may I make one further suggestion? If the government will come forward with something more of a constructive nature that is going to help this country, so far as this party is concerned we shall be glad to sit here indefinitely to put it through; but I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the government are out of touch with the people and not in a position to know their wishes. I suggest, finally, that the Prime Minister, when the visit of their majesties is over, dissolve parliament at the earliest possible moment so that we may get a government with a mandate from the people which will do something constructive for the country.

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT

speechtext:
The house resumed from Tuesday, May 9, consideration in committee of Bill No. 83, to assist agriculture in the prairie provinces-Mr. Gardiner-Mr. Sanderson in the chair.
On section 4-Crop failure assistance.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it was suggested last night that a revision be made in subsection (1) of section 4. I will ask one of my colleagues to move, in amendment:
That section 4 be amended by deleting the whole of subsection 1 and substituting therefor the following:
"The governor in council may, whenever the minister finds that the average yield of wheat as a result of anything other than hail is five bushels per acre or less in each of not less than one hundred and thirty-five townships in any one province in the spring wheat area, declare such area to be a crop failure area."

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext: I move accordingly.

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext: The reason for the change is to meet the suggestion made last night, without interfering with the intention of the original subsection. There are three causes for reduction of yield over a considerable area in the west which have resulted in crop failures-hail, drought, and grasshoppers.

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext: Rust.

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext:
There are other causes over limited areas, for crop failures, but they could not be considered as of national scope. Hail is taken care of through hail insurance, over a considerable part of the west. Insurance against hail has been arranged by muni-71492-241
cipalities and by private companies. At this time I do not believe this legislation should interfere with activities in the west in connection with hail insurance, so I am suggesting that hail should not be covered by this particular section.

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext:
In introducing this
amendment the minister said he did not wish to detract from the principle as originally set out, but was rather trying to meet the views expressed yesterday by some hon. members. He said that in certain areas crop failures were due to hail, drought and grasshoppers, but that hail had been taken care of by municipal bodies, provincial governments or hail insurance companies. But the point hon. members in this corner of the house had in mind was not so much the amount of grain one may get; it was the question of the value the farmer received from his crop, no matter what the yield might be. We have stated over and over again that a farmer might have only five bushels to the acre of No. 1 wheat, and yet be much better off than a farmer who has ten bushels of poor grade wheat. The new amendment therefore does not in any way meet the suggestions we have made.
Subsection 3 of section 4 states:
The Peace River district of the province of British Columbia and the province of Alberta shall, for the purpose of this section, be deemed to be one province.
In order to qualify for crop failure assistance, it is necessary that in any province there shall be not less than 135 townships with a crop of five bushels to the acre or less. The minister knows very well that assistance of that kind is not possible in an area such as the Peace River district, either in Alberta or in British Columbia. Up to the present time drought has been known only to a very limited degree in the Peace River area. I believe last year there were certain areas-

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext: The hon. member should be thankful for that.

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext:
We are thankful indeed. In the areas surrounding Wembley and Grande Prairie, which always produce good crops, last year there was some drought and the yield was low. Nevertheless over the whole Peace River district that condition does not recur year after year, as happens in various other parts of the prairie provinces. The whole area of the Peace River country in Alberta and British Columbia is going to be penalized because of its preferred position. Our trouble is not from drought or grasshoppers-at least it has not been up to the present time. We do not get the same return as people who

Prairie Farm Assistance

have the best grades of grain, because sometimes our grain is subjected to frost and the return is not as high as that of the man who harvests five bushels per acre of Manitoba No. 1 wheat, and who lives close to Winnipeg or to some other market in western Canada.
In addition, every hon. member knows that the Peace River district pays a higher freight rate on grain than any other district in Canada. The northern parts of Alberta and British Columbia are the heaviest contributors per hundred pounds, so far as freight rates on grain are concerned, of any group in the country. Simply because we happen to be a good part of Canada, and simply because we happen to have a good yield, we are now being compelled to pay a levy. This is not a tax; it is called a levy, and we are compelled to pay that levy and in addition must be discriminated against because of the high freight rate we have to pay.
This type of legislation is most unfair. It falls most heavily on individuals who have been able to keep on their own feet. After all, time and time again in the House of Commons we have been told that drought in the western provinces is a national calamity. We have been told that drought is a national problem; appeals have been made to eastern Canada on that ground, and support has been given in the light of that understanding. Now we no longer say it is a national problem, but we attempt to penalize a good portion of the people of western Canada, people who have produced continuously.
I repeat that the Peace River district in Alberta and British Columbia can never fall within the conditions outlined in the bill. There never have been 135 townships in the Peace River district of Alberta and British Columbia which have had less than five bushels to the acre. But if this measure passes, year after year we will pay the percentage levy in addition to the discrimination in freight charges.
I hope the minister will reconsider this part of the bill. We do not oppose the principle of crop insurance, provided we too can benefit from it. There are certain portions of the Peace River country which might be affected, but we have had good crops and we hope they will always continue. I repeat, there might come a time when certain portions of the district might not be able to grow crops as good as the ones grown at the present time. We should like to share to a certain degree the wealth and the better growing conditions that we have in the Peace River country, but I submit that we have been penalized by freight rates and tariffs and other things and it is most unfair to put the additional burden 
of this type of crop insurance legislation upon these people. After all they are pioneers and were supposed to be given every possible encouragement.
We have here legislation dealing with conditions which cannot possibly prevail in the type of country such as the northern part of British Columbia and the northern part of Alberta. Section 4 states definitely that the Peace River district is taken away from Alberta and, along with the northern part of British Columbia, is to be called a province for the purposes of this legislation. What does that mean? It means that the Peace River area is entirely precluded from qualifying under this legislation. As I say, from time to time certain portions of the Peace River country may suffer, but I cannot conceive that 135 townships in that country will ever have crops of less than five bushels to the acre. The present freight rates are discriminatory against the Peace River country and we shall have to continue to pay for something from which we will receive no benefit whatever. Drought on the prairies is not a sectional problem; it is national in scope. I think the minister should reconsider this part of his proposed legislation.

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext: I understood the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Pelletier) to suggest that the adding of the Peace River district would exclude that district from the benefits of this particular section. The very opposite is the case. The Peace River district is being added to Alberta, so it will be possible for the district to come under the operation of this section as though it were a part of Alberta.

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext:
That is not what the
subsection says. It reads:
The Peace River district of the province of British Columbia and the province of Alberta shall, for the purposes of this section, be deemed to be one province.

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext: The whole province of Alberta and the Peace River district of British Columbia.

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext: That is not clear at all. If the minister is willing to state definitely that that part of British Columbia shall become part of the province of Alberta for the purposes of this section, it puts a different angle on the matter.

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext: That is what it means for the purposes of this legislation. That is the only reason for putting it there.

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext:
I believe that the farmers living in these drought damaged depressed areas and who have been suffering all these

Prairie Farm Assistance
years should be given adequate protection, but I do not think this bill is going about it in the right way. Section 4 sets out the conditions for declaring an area a crop failure area, and deals with matters of acreage and geography. In my opinion, no minister should have the responsibility of administering the provisions of this section. They are judicial in character and relate to public policy as well as to finance. This section provides for the award which will be made to a farmer suffering from drought or damage by grasshoppers. In my opinion the wheat board should administer not only this bill but all the others, and not the governor in council or the minister. It would be an impartial board, and the minister would be well advised to put a man like Mr. John McFarland at its head in respect of this and all other bills of the kind. This year seems to be the annus mirabilis so far as the minister is concerned, or year of wonders.
The minister is to be given a blank cheque to cover awards to be paid to the farmers. No minister of the crown should be charged with the duty of deciding the area or the conditions. The minister may say whether a particular district shall come under this legislation, or whether or not a particular municipality or group of municipalities shall benefit. Section 4 deals directly with the municipalities. and the minister may deal with the townships or many of them making up a municipality. One principle, that of direct dealing with municipalities, is being carried out in this section, while other principles are beng carried out in other relief bills of the Labour department. Last session I raised the question of these drought areas and asked that an inquiry be held to see if some longterm policy could not be adopted in respect to them. I pointed out in the house and in the committee that the United States had adopted the use of machinery to a greater extent than any other country in the world. The United States farmer turned his machines on the timber, and he now finds himself confronted with rising waters in the shape of floods and falling waters in the shape of drought. Instead of having a lot of college professors on the prairies who argue not from facts but from opinions deal with this problem, further investigation should be made by actual experts as to its causes and some longterm policjr should be adopted to remedy it. There has been some criticism of hon. members from Ontario who sit on this side of the house. Let me say we here have been the pioneers of legislation to aid the west by protection all along the line when those opposite were for free trade-we were all pioneers in
71492-241J
direct relief when needed. To use Disraeli's words, the Liberal government found the Conservatives in bathing and have appropriated their clothes. That is what has happened in connection with this and other bills of the former free traders-the Liberals on the prairies. We advocated crop failure assistance as far back as May 5, 1924. We asked for protection for the farmer along these lines, and hon. gentlemen opposite, yes and hon. members of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, or the Progressives, when their leader was the present Minister of Mines and Resources, were all for free trade in this particular trade. They did not want to protect the farmer. I said the best friend of the western wheat grower was the policy of protection. At that time I said:
I am here to argue for protection because of my conviction that the only hope of profitable wheat growing in western Canada or any part of Canada is in a system of protection that will give the Canadian wheat grower a quality price for his quality crop.
And again:
Leave the wheat growing industry of the west to the workings of the law of supply and demand and that law would not fill the west with wheat growers. If that law did fill the west with wheat growers, wheat would not be worth 50 cents a bushel.
I argued then for an extension of that protection policy for the grain grower in all its forms. A long discussion took place at that time as to what form this protection should take. I am glad to see the minister and those who sit with him come to our views and our policies, as we were the pioneers in it. I am glad to see the members of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation now contending that protection should be given to the grain industry. They did not then believe in the policy of protection for grain advocated by the Conservative party consistently ever since confederation.
The last line of subsection 1 states that the governor in council may declare an area to be a crop failure area. Why is it that the government has changed the system? Why should the governor in council, a political agency, do this instead of a permanent board like the wheat board? Why give the minister a blank cheque to make these awards? The second subsection reads:
Provided that no award under this section shall be made to a farmer in any township in which the average yield of wheat has been found by the minister to be eight bushels or more per acre.
This is an omnibus bill and an omnibus method of making these awards. I ask the hon. member for Weyburn to look up the words that I used on May 5, 1924 as to the
Prairie Farm Assistance

policy of his party for free trade all along the line for grain, when the Minister of Mines and Resources was leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation in this house- then the Progressive Liberals. Hon. gentlemen opposite have for many years been wearing a coat of many colours in connection with the grain industry and its protection, and I am glad that at last they realize that this industry needs protection all along the line as I proposed on May 5, 1924.

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext: I have no wish to be unfair, but I must point out that while the amendment changes the factors to be considered in arriving at the causes for the reduced yield-it helps in that way and may help the minister to win an argument-it does not completely meet the real needs of the situation. The one province, the one large section of the country that can ordinarily qualify at any time on a bushel basis, is Saskatchewan. Alberta and Manitoba only once in a long time can come within the qualifications, and that would be in an extreme drought year such as 1937. But in a year when frost, rust and other conditions which considerably reduce yield are present, and would affect us seriously in northern and central Alberta, the hardship is just as great to the farmers as if they had only five bushels to the acre, because their cash yield might be less than five bushels at 80 cents, which would be $4. Neither Manitoba nor Alberta can meet these qualifications. I doubt whether in any year, except one in which there is a complete disaster, there would be 135 townships in Alberta with five bushels to the acre or less. History does not show anything of the kind.

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext: The year before last.

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext: Just one time.

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext: And many other times.

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext: If the government really believes in the principle of crop insurance, and is genuine in its belief, why not apply it equitably? Why not make it a matter of the value of five bushels to the acre? You cannot have it both ways. If you are going to have the 135 townships, you must give us the other qualification. On the other hand, if you are going to have the five bushels to the acre, you must reduce the number of townships. Otherwise it is not fair to Alberta or Manitoba.

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext:
I think there is only one ground upon which that argument might be partly correct. It is not on the ground that Saskatchewan is not more afflicted by rust than Alberta. As a matter of fact, Saskatche-

wan has been more seriously afflicted by both grasshoppers and rust than either of the other two provinces-and particularly by rust. Rust takes the southwestern part of Manitoba; only in one year did it take Manitoba without taking a much larger area in Saskatchewan, and that was the first year that we had rust, many years ago. As all of us in western Canada know, every year that we have rust it extends a little further northward and westward, and it has gone all the way across Saskatchewan in the last three periods of rust and has touched Alberta slightly on the last two occasions. Saskatchewan is very much more afflicted by rust than Alberta. So there is no real point in the argument that by eliminating rust, as we did in the first draft of the legislation, we were assisting Saskatchewan. In addition, it is very seldom, except in years like last year when rust accompanied by grasshoppers takes certain areas, that rust has taken the entire crop. Usually a rusted crop is not reduced to five bushels. Rust comes usually when you have a very heavy stand of grain. It seldom comes to a light crop. When you have a heavy crop and rust comes in July, it seldom reduces the crop to five bushels; it is more likely to be fifteen or twelve bushels.

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext: Would it be worth four dollars to the acre?

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext: It might easily be worth much more than that. So far as the records show, Alberta would have benefited by this legislation on quite a number of occasions in the last eighteen years.

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext: With the 135 townships?

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext: In what years were there 135 townships in Alberta with less than five bushels to the acre?

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext:
The year before last was the last one. I have not the records here, but I presume the same would apply to 1931. In two out of the three years that I have had charge of the department Alberta has been in; it could not be in unless they had twenty-five municipalities to come in the first place, and this is only fifteen. Manitoba had fourteen during part of the time, and, during the remainder of the year nineteen only three years ago. The records I have here are the records on the map, eighteen-year records. If you go up to sixteen bushels, Manitoba has come under that almost as often as any other part of western Canada during that time. The only section that probably would not be dealt with as we are dealing

Prairie Farm Assistance
with the remainder of the areas would be the Peace River country, for which the hon. member for the district was speaking; but they have only 300,000 acres of wheat in that country. As I said last evening, after one year's experience with this legislation, when we have the records from all over that area, it may be advisable to consider eliminating certain of these well-defined areas such as the Peace River country. I do not think anyone will seriously object to our making a small levy this year while we are gathering the information, in view of the fact that a special price was paid by the government last year and the payment possibly will be repeated this year for areas that have these crops. Of course if the levy under the legislation were removed from any area in the future the benefits would also be removed.

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext: Do I understand the minister to state that he no longer believes that drought in western Canada is a national problem, but that it must be provided for out of the funds of the western farmer? Is that what he is contending for?

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman, that does not follow. The provision that is being made for the raising of funds from wheat would not provide for more than one-eighth of what would have been necessary to meet the situation existing last year had this legislation been in effect. In other words, it would have taken eight to ten years without any money being paid out of the fund to accumulate sufficient to take care of the year 1937-38. I do not think anyone supposes that the condition is going to be difficult in the future. In other words, part of the money will be collected from the farmers themselves, and all the farmers of western Canada with whom I have discussed the matter are prepared to pay the amount necessary to assist to take care of them in the difficult years.

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext: Where will the rest come from?

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext: Out of the treasury.

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext: In the form of a loan?

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext: A loan without interest. It is only refunded by these payments, and if there are not sufficient payments, as there would not be according to this figuring, then of course it is never paid back by the farmer.

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext: It becomes a debt.

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext:
It becomes a debt
charge on the treasury of Canada.

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext:
There is a phase of
the proposal which does not appeal to me
as very acceptable. Yesterday the Minister of Agriculture remarked several times that if, for instance, in a province only six or eight municipalities were affected, that province would be expected to take care of the situation. That is what I understood. It is just possible that a province may have up to fourteen municipalities in that position, so that many years might elapse before it would receive any revenue from this fund. But in the meanwhile the province takes care of anywhere from one to fourteen municipalities and gets no remuneration from this fund. It seems to me that there is an injustice in such a situation, in that while funds are taken from the province, the province is expected to take care of those municipalities.

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext:
Well, as was observed
last evening by an hon. member, investigations have been carried on in the provinces over a number of years, apparently with a view of having set up a crop insurance plan of some kind. These provinces have at no time thought that a province by itself could set up that insurance plan. They have been advocating that the federal government should come into the picture at some stage and pay a part of those costs, but none of the provinces has ever contended that the federal government should take care of all that kind of assistance; their view was that when it became too big a task for the province to undertake alone, the federal government should come in and assist. That has always been their contention with regard to crop failure, and under these circumstances we have always intervened and given assistance. Now they have advocated exactly the same thing in connection with crop insurance, and we are saying to them by this legislation that we are prepared to assume the national obligation, but we think at the same time the provinces should be prepared also to assume an obligation in connection with the matter. I have no doubt that when this legislation is placed on the statute book and is operating, we shall have proposals from the provinces making it possible for them to take care of that proportion of this assist ance which we think should bear upon the province.

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext: I have here some information which has a very direct bearing upon this matter and which has just arrived from the bureau of statistics; it was asked for since the discussion last night. It is a table defining the area from which no crop was harvested because of crop failure.

speechtext:
In what year?

speechtext:

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext: I do not want an argument to be based on something which is not absolutely sound. There would be that many acres, but not that many acres of wheat. Only a percentage of the acreage in a township would be in wheat.

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext: That might be very true.

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext: It would be absolutely true.

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext: But certainly it does not affect at all my argument that if you base your qualification for relief under this measure on a five bushel to the acre yield of wheat, you are not carrying out the intention of the legislation.

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext:
On the other hand, the figures which the hon. member is giving are of absolute crop failure; that is, no grain at all.

When you go up to five bushels to the acre you will add four or five times that area in some years.

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext:
Well, no crop was
harvested, because of crop failure.

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext: No crop at all?

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext: A crop of four bushels to the acre would not be worth harvesting.

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext: Certainly not. It bears out the argument I have been making all along, that if 3,110.400 acres of land in wheat crops must have less than five bushels to the acre to qualify under this bill, it represents an impossible position in a very large part of our wheat-growing country, except in a very few exceedingly calamitous years. If, of course, it is the intention of the bill to deal only with conditions in one or two very calamitous years in the course of a century, you are going to achieve that result. If you really want to deal with the problem the qualification for bonus under this act must be on a value per acre yield basis; otherwise the act will not be of any benefit to the farmers.

speechtext: I do not like to interrupt the hon. gentleman, but he is discussing section 5 and we are on an amendment to section 4.

I beg your pardon, Mr. Chairman. I did not intend to discuss section 5. I was simply pointing out that section 4 need not be amended to meet
the objections of the members from Alberta if the minister would keep the point in mind in forming the regulations.
I wish to emphasize one matter that is of importance, and that is size. The point is well taken by those from Alberta and Manitoba, and it is not for me to stress it on the question of the 135 townships. The minister mentioned that proportionately the numbers of crop failures in Saskatchewan have not been greater than in the other provinces. Now if you say that the crop failure area shall be fifteen municipalities in Saskatchewan, then according to this argument it ought to be eight in Manitoba, or Alberta, because their proportion of land under crop is relatively smaller. I do not wish to see Saskatchewan faced with any greater difficulty with respect to qualification than the other two provinces, but I submit that there is a case for those provinces in this regard, and it might be that ten municipalities in the other two provinces would bear a reasonable relationship to the number fixed in Saskatchewan. Would the 135 townships have to be contiguous, a solid bloc?
Anywhere at all in the province.

We are reluctant to leave this section because it is of such vast importance. I do not want the minister to get the impression that we are opposed to the scheme of crop insurance. We are trying to arrive at conditions that shall be fair over as wide a territory as possible. Frankly, so far as we from Alberta are concerned, I may say that we have already dealt with a similar scheme of crop insurance. The provincial government attempted to do something of the kind some time ago. In that province there was talk at one time of providing crop insurance to cover all kinds of crop failure, no matter from what cause it might arise, whether drought, hail, floods, rust or anything else. The fund was to be built up by a three per cent levy, but it was felt that the levy was too high, and I believe, although I am not sure, that the government of Alberta came to the conclusion that the matter should receive further consideration and therefore they did not 
proceed with the plan. The plan was very similar to the one which the minister now proposes, namely, that there should be a levy to take care of certain crop failures.
We are in sympathy with the minister in this measure and we intend to support it. We simply wish to amplify some of our views. We think that there are certain portions of the bill which bear unequally upon the population of western Canada and they should be rectified. We are willing to accept the contention that experience will indicate more than we know now and as the years pass we shall be in a better position to judge what amendments should be introduced. We simply say that at this time 135 townships in any one province is much too large an area, and the computation should be made on the basis of value, that is, the equivalent of five bushels in value instead of simply stipulating five bushels. We are not putting forward these views in any spirit of criticism. We support the principle of the bill, and we think that these ideas that we are putting forward should be incorporated in a bill of this type.

If the committee will permit me I should like to withdraw the amendment that has been proposed, and to offer the following:
That section 4 be amended by deleting the whole of subsection (1) and substituting therefor the following:
"(1) The governor in council may, whenever the minister finds that the average yield of wheat, as a result of anything other than hail, is five bushels per acre or less in each of not less than one hundred and thirty-five townships in Saskatchewan, one hundred in each of the provinces of Alberta and Manitoba declare such provincial area to be a crop failure area."
In Alberta and in Manitoba 100 townships is 11% municipalities.
I move that amendment.
That amendment will tend to meet the point for the present, but we should like to see the computation made on the basis of value. Perhaps that would be expecting too much.
Amendment agreed to.

I suggest an amendment to subsection 2, not making any change, but to clarify it. A number of legal members of the house have called my attention to the possibility of misunderstanding in the subsection as drafted. The amendment is:
That section 4 be amended by deleting the whole of subsection 2 and substituting therefor the following:
"(2) The minister may, subject as in this act provided, with the approval of the governor in

Prairie Farm Assistance
council, award to each farmer in a crop failure area by way of assistance a sum of two hundred dollars or a sum not exceeding two dollars and fifty cents per acre with respect to half the cultivated acreage of the farmer not to exceed two hundred acres, whichever is the greater."
That makes it clear, I think. It means the same thing.
The original drafting was certainly not clear.
This is my drafting.
I so move.
Amendment agreed to.

I should like to make a comment before the clause is carried. May I hasten to express to the minister our deep appreciation of his consideration in making this modification for us. We believe that we are even now suffering an injustice in Alberta, but none the less we feel grateful for the adjustment which has been made. I want to make it clear that we have no objection to helping Saskatchewan. We in the west are struggling against fearful odds the magnitude of which I believe very few appreciate, perhaps even there. We want to help each other, but we must make it clear to the people that we must have assistance from the federal government on a rather generous scale if we are to survive the hardships by which we are faced. There seems to be an idea conveyed by the minister-I am not sure that I understood his intention aright-that the province should be prepared to bear a good deal of the hardship which comes from crop failures. It must be emphasized, and laboured to the point where we all realize it, that when moneys are paid from the federal treasury to an area in Alberta the province of Alberta is already contributing a share of those revenues which are being paid out. And the same is true for other provinces. It is not as though the money being given by the federal government were coming from six provinces only; it is coming from all nine provinces. I have observed too great a tendency on the part of hon. members to forget this. Through the sales tax we are contributing a tremendous sum of money. We are contributing through the tariff a tremendous sum; we are doing perhaps more than our share in supporting the railroads; we are contributing our full share of the one cent extra on the three cent stamp for postage, and we are contributing our share of excise tax and a great number of other taxes, the total of which I shall probably refer to by and by but not at the moment. But when the total is finally computed it will reach proportions which will astonish hon. members. So that
when we as a province ask that a share of that be returned to us in our time of need, we are asking only what we have a just right to ask.

But it must be remembered that it is grossly unfair to require farmers in an area to be constantly contributing and never receiving anything in return, especially if in years when they do have a mishap their province may not qualify because of an insufficient number of townships.
If it is insurance I would say they are lucky if they never get a return.

I would grant that, but at the same time these men must contribute one cent a bushel, and it would amount to a large sum in a year such as 1928 when the yield was 52-1 bushels, or in 1915 when it was 63-1 bushels. That may be true. But those people are contributing a tremendous amount of money towards funds which should be used to relieve them in time of need. I think that is a matter which ought to be taken into consideration. It would be altogether different if a man were voluntarily entering into an insurance scheme. If he fails to get results under those circumstances he at least has a sort of gambler's chance. But there is no alternative here. In my constituency, for example, it does not matter a particle whether or not the grain on which the one cent a bushel is being paid-
We have not reached that section yet.

Just the same, it is all involved. It matters not a particle whether the grain on which one cent a bushel is being collected is being produced two miles or forty miles from the elevator; there is an unfairness here which ultimately I know the minister-

On a point of order; we are now discussing whether or not payment should be made under section 4. If the hon. member for Lethbridge agrees with that section we might pass it, and proceed to a discussion of section 5.

Shall section 4 as
