speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: What section is the hon. member discussing?
I am discussing subsection 3 of section 4. In any event, I am talking about the Peace River district of British Columbia. I am sure the minister knows to what I refer.
Yes.

I was pleased to hear the distinction made a moment ago by the .minister. I would suggest, however, that he make use of his legal department once more in order to make this subsection clearer than it is at the present time. There must be some room for misunderstanding in view of the way it is now worded. I am not saying it should be changed, but I am making the 
suggestion it should be clarified so that there could be no difficulty of interpretation later on. I mention this matter-
It is clear now.

No, it is not too clear. The section uses the words "Peace River district of the province of British Columbia and the province of Alberta." There is a Peace River district in Alberta, too. It is in one area, really. The section might be open to the interpretation placed upon it by the hon. member when he first spoke, and I would suggest the words "the Peace River district of the province of British Columbia shall for the purpose of this section be deemed to be part of the province of Alberta". That would cover the intended meaning.
That would be clear; as a matter of fact those are the words I had intended to suggest, and I believe they will meet the difficulty I have pointed out.
British Columbia was anxious to take on the Yukon; why can they not take on the Peace River area?

I believe the words
might be reversed in this way, to meet the approval of all:
The province of Alberta and the Peace River district of the province of British Columbia shall for the purposes of this section be deemed to be one province.
That is even better.

I so
move.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 5-Regulations by minister.

I would draw the attention of the minister to paragraph (g), containing these words:
(g) excluding from the operation of this act farmers who do not reside upon farms, within the meaning of the regulation.
Would a renter come within the benefit of that paragraph?

No, he would not come under that. He would come under the section which makes it possible for us to define by regulation a resident farmer. That paragraph has to do more particularly with lands on which we are spending money for irrigation purposes, and which would not come under this particular section.

Would the
minister state the condition with respect to a

Prairie Farm Assistance
renter? How would they get their income? Would it be divided up partly with the owner?

There is in the bill a definition which states that a farmer means a person engaged in farming in the spring wheat area. Then paragraph (g) excludes from the operation of the act farmers who do not reside upon farms within the meaning of the regulation.

What about
the renter?
The renter would come under this.

Would the
income go to him or to the man who owns the farm?

The intention of the
bill is that it should go to the renter.
In certain parts of Saskatchewan the people live in villages and farm the surrounding territory.

That is exactly what
this is intended for. It would exclude from the operation of the bill a farmer who does not reside on his farm in the manner required, but the manner required would include the man living within the bounds of a village but farming outside the village. He would be considered a resident fanner.
He	would be?
Yes.

As the hon. member for
Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) rose in his place I was going to ask the minister how this would affect the tenant farmer. In many instances a hardship would be worked, especially if a landlord insisted on his share of the crop no matter how small the yield. There should be something to protect the tenant farmer, and I should like to know what that protection will be.

A later section in the
bill states that the amount shall not be attachable by anyone. The only way in which an owner of land could obtain a right to this money would be through the lease he has with the individual. This money is not intended for the purpose of paying part of the value of the crop, it is for the purpose of assisting the man who is actually farming the land to stay on the land. He gets all the money, but if he pays it over to someone else it is his own affair.
He is protected under section S.

This is the section that .
gives the minister power to set out regulations and rules, and I think it will involve some difficulty. The minister is to provide regulations providing the manner in which average yields of wheat shall be ascertained, as well as regulations in connection with the acreage cultivated in a municipality. There may be instances where a municipality would like to increase the land under cultivation, but on the other hand, if the average yield is kept as low as possible, it might help as far as relief was concerned. I think the minister would be well advised to watch that the municipalities do not overstep the mark, so to speak, in this respect. I understand that as far as possible he is going to use the municipality as the unit in arriving at the average yield and the number of acres under cultivation in a township. I suggest that he be very careful to see that the administration of this legislation is carried out in such a way that the municipalities will not be able to carry on as we know they did last winter in the northern part of Saskatchewan with respect to relief. It might easily happen that if they had no yield and a large acreage, the municipality would be helped in taking care of some of their ratepayers.

Under this
section the minister may make regulations requiring farmers to furnish information as specified in such regulations and providing the manner in which the average yields of wheat shall be ascertained by the minister.
I think most of us have been anxious to know just how the minister proposes to gather the information with reference to the average yields. Is this information going to be collected by the municipal secretary, or are questionnaires to be sent to the individual farmers? The value of this measure will depend upon how the average yield in any township is going to be declared, because if a township does not qualify, the farmers in that township receive no benefits.

I cannot state what
the final regulations will be, but they will all be gone into carefully. In connection with the point raised by the hon, member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley), I do not assume that the department will depend upon the information received from the municipality in order to reach a decision. The suggestion I made yesterday was that the federal government will probably not be very much concerned about an area within a municipality unless the municipal council calls our attention to the fact that there is a low yield in

Prairie Farm Assistance
the municipality. That is where the first request would come from. They would say, "We have so many townships in our municipalities that have yields of five bushels or less to the acre." We would probably follow the practice which was followed in connection with relief and say, "You make an application to the province," and when the province tells us that there are 100 townships in Alberta, 100 in Manitoba, or 135 in Saskatchewan, with yields of less than five bushels to the acre, we would go and check those townships. But we would do the checking to find out whether the yield was under five bushels. We will not be very much concerned about going into a township unless either the municipality or the province draws our attention to the fact that the yield is low. As soon as they do draw our attention to that, we will have a check made.
With regard to the first paragraph which refers to regulations requiring farmers to furnish information as specified in such regulations, I imagine that the practice here will be the general practice which has been followed in connection with hail insurance. Everyone who lives in a municipality in the west having hail insurance receives in May or June a blue sheet of paper upon which is the design of a section of land. The farmer marks out his acreage and what he has on it and sends it back. Those are filed as a matter of record. If there is no reason for payment to be made, those records would simply be filed, but if it is necessary to make a check in the fall of the year, the information as to yield will be available. The provincial hail organizations have these records and there should be no difficulty about our getting the same records.
That covers the part of my question which had to do with crop failure assistance, but what about a national emergency?

It would be the same
thing.

You would
have a more complicated problem. There may be two townships side by side, and it would make all the difference in the world whether the average yield in a township was six or four bushels to the acre. There would be a difference in the bonus, and this would have to be computed very closely or there would be considerable dispute and difficulty.

There is a margin of four bushel averages in the division. A suggestion has been made by some who have not had any experience in the matter, because

it has not been dealt with in this way, that in connection with crop yields the fairest division would be two bushel averages instead of four. I believe, however, that if we went out at this time without any information and tried to make a division of that kind it would be extremely complicated. The legislation is now drawn on the basis of four bushels, and probably we may find from experience that it would be better to make that division two. Some people say it ought to be made one, but I doubt that. I think two is about as far as we will ever go, and that may have to be done in future years.

How are you going to get anything approximating the average return in a township where a large farm might be partly in one township and partly in another? Are you going to have individual returns from every farmer or from every elevator? I think that is where the cause of complaint will be. People will claim that a certain township has a higher average than it is given credit for, or it may be claimed that another township is being credited with a lower average than it really has.

Legislation was introduced in the Saskatchewan legislature this year which would compel thresher-men to send in returns at the end of the threshing season. The bill was finally withdrawn after a great deal of discussion had taken place. But it was no doubt intended to be the forerunner of legislation which might be brought in to deal with this very matter. Whether that can be done in future sessions of the western legislatures is a question yet to be considered. In any event one can obtain the services of men who can drive through any township and, inside of forty-eight hours' driving, tell you just about as closely as you will figure it after you have threshed the grain what the average yield in that township will be. Every year men drive over the whole area from the gulf of Mexico to the far north and report back to the city of Chicago, giving estimates upon which we base all our discussions with regard to wheat. They can tell you closely what the yield is likely to be merely by driving through a district and examining the heads in a few fields.
Except for grasshoppers.

They destroy the grain very quickly, and you do not need to do much figuring about that.

Prairie Farm Assistance
Last year a section or a quarter section that looked pretty good from the road would 'be found destroyed by grasshoppers when examined closely.
These men examine all these things.

Some farmers may be on heavy clay soils, and others on light soils. Sixty per cent of the land may be heavy and forty per cent light; and on the sixty per cent heavy land the average yield would be, say, twenty bushels to the acre, while on the lighter soil it might be five bushels to the acre. Will any allowance be made for that?

When we have the records for all three provinces as we have now for Saskatchewan, it is possible that the proper thing to do would be what they are attempting to do in certain parts of the United States, that is, instead of working on the basis of townships, work on the basis of soil-condition areas. When one flies over the west in a plane to-day, one can see the bounds of these areas underneath, if one knows the nature of the soil; and that whole country can be mapped, as it is being mapped to-day by photographers in aeroplanes. We can eventually do that, but we have not that information now. So the township is the best possible basis to work on to get our principles established.
There have been soil surveys of a number of areas.

I think it would be wise to provide that all orders in council and regulations made under this measure be published in the Canada Gazette. A provision could be inserted to read:
All orders in council and all regulations made under the provisions of this act or an abstract thereof disclosing their essential provisions shall be published in the next following issue of the Canada Gazette.
That would come at the end.
Yes.

Paragraph (f) of section 5 is not as clear as it should be. It reads:
(f) providing that in special circumstances another kind of grain may be taken in lieu of wheat as the basis of awards under this act, and in that event what number of bushels of such other kind of grain shall be deemed to be equivalent to a certain number of bushels of wheat for the purposes of such substitution.
It is necessary to get the equivalent to enable the minister to determine the conditions for declaring an area a crop failure area,
which conditions are fully set out in section 4. That is the minister's intention, but are the words in paragraph (f) of section 5, "a certain number of bushels of wheat" clear? Would it not be better to state a definite number of bushels of wheat, as is done in section 4? I think if you said something like "deemed to be equivalent to five bushels to the acre of wheat or less," the clause would be clearer.

It would be very difficult to do that in advance because it might have to be changed from time to time. So it is better to leave it to regulation. There is no relationship, for instance, between prices of rye and wheat to-day, compared with those of fifteen or twenty years ago, when rye was selling sometimes higher than wheat. Then the price of rye gradually came down until it is selling now more in line with barley. All these matters would have to be taken into consideration. You cannot put all that in the bill.
If you put in the bill "five bushels," it would apply only to the crop failure assistance section, while it should apply to the national emergency clause as well.
It is intended to apply to both.

Paragraph (g) states:
(g) excluding from the operation of this act farmers who do not reside upon farms, within the meaning of the regulation.
Many farmers do not actually live on the land.

Take market gardeners living near cities. There are quite a number of them who are enumerated in the census as being farmers farming land under fifty acres. Many of them are not growing grain, and if they put in ten acres of grain they could come under the legislation, unless prevented by regulation.

I am wondering about several people in the minister's own neighbourhood at Balgonie, Pense and other places where farmers are not actually living on the lands they farm but in a nearby village. Would this clause exclude them?

No, it makes it possible for them not to be excluded. If we had said in the definition of farmer that the man had to live on his farm, they would have been excluded. We deal with the matter by regulation.

What is being done by paragraph (g) is to place in the hands of
Prairie Farm Assistance

the minister the power to say who shall and who shall not be benefited by this legislation. It is a power about which it is difficult to express my opinion without giving offence-
It is in the hands of council, not the minister.
The minister may make regulations-
With the approval of the governor in council.

The minister may make regulations excluding from the operation of the legislation farmers who do not reside upon farms. There is no restriction upon what the minister may do in that regard, except, of course, that he has to carry the judgment of his colleagues. There is nothing in the statute that says who shall and who shall not be entitled to "benefit, and I object very much to the breadth of this power of regulation.
What will be the position of a number of land companies farming land in and around Regina, for instance? Would they be excluded by paragraph (g)
Some of them, I hope, would be. It is intended to assist those living on the land.
I hope that in drawing up regulations the minister will not exclude farmers farming fifty acres if they are making their living by growing grain.

Take the Indian Head district, which the minister knows very well. Many men live in Indian Head and drive out to their farms two or three miles away. They are really conducting all the farming operations and paying the men. The farms are not even rented. All the expenses are met by the land owner. He is really the farmer but is living in Indian Head. There are many such men in my home town of Wolseley. Would they be excluded? They should not be because they are making as good a contribution to the country as anybody.

We had a definition of farmer in the bill as first drafted. But to define farmer would exclude the very men of whom the hon. member speaks. That is why the matter is left to regulations. The hon. member for Kootenay East speaks as though the minister might deal with individuals, but no minister would undertake, not even in the government of which he was a member, to go that far. It would cause so

much trouble that he would not get very far with it. But in regulations you deal with certain groups of people and see that this particular group or that are bona fide farmers. These officials will administer the measure accordingly. As to whether the group which the hon. member for Qu'Appelle has in mind would come directly under the terms of this, I am not in a position to say at the moment. Probably some of them would and some of them would not.

Would it
mean that some official out there in the country who will be administering the legislation would help to determine to some extent whether a man would come under this?
No; the regulations will determine what an official will do out in the country. The regulations will be passed by order in council.
I am thinking of my own case. I farm three different farms. I do not live on any of them; I live three miles away, in the city.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, are you a farmer?
I certainly am. I do not do anything except farming, and this.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is the test. That is the real test.
If that is the ruling. I am satisfied to leave it in the hands of the minister.

Section agreed to.
On section 6-Levy of one per centum from purchase price of all grain purchased by licencees.

This is another important clause. Under section 3 the change made by the minister really cuts by about one-half the benefits which may be given to the farmer as a relief measure, as compared with the original draft. I look upon this bill as more or less a relief measure. True enough, there is an element of insurance in it, but I regard it largely as a measure of relief. As I have said, I think it was yesterday, I am in favour of the principle. I am also in favour of the insurance principle. I do not believe, however, that the time is opportune to impose a one per cent levy on the producers. What many of them will get will be a mere pittance, and they will not have enough to carry on. I have made a rough estimate of the cost on the basis of last year's crop, and I think it would work out for the whole west at about 11-2 cents an acre and would bring in nearly

Prairie Farm Assistance
$2,800,000. I suggest that the minister would be well advised to reduce this levy, if not to cut it out altogether.

This levy will be made only against the man who markets his wheat. Yesterday the minister told us that in the last year or two he had fed his crop to hogs. The man who sells his wheat through hogs, as the minister put it yesterday, will get the benefit of this legislation in the event of crop failure, but he will not make any contribution because he does not sell his wheat through the elevator.
He might sell his rye.
Well, let us deal now with this wheat question. How will the minister, if he continues to sell his wheat through hogs, make a contribution to the fund?

The wheat which would be fed to hogs would not be No. 1 or No. 2 northern, it would only be feed wheat, No. 5 or No. 6, which should never be ground into flour at all. Those are grades which should be ground into hog feed.

What the
minister's opinion is will not count unless the legislation provides for it. These people will draw the benefits of this bill by virtue of the fact that they are growing wheat, if they have a crop failure, but if they do not market the wheat through the usual channels, but feed it to stock, they will not pay their one per cent.
Are they all Scotsmen out there?

The hon. member for
Lethbridge showed how the levy would fall very heavily on people in certain districts. It would fall heavily on the district round Lethbridge which he mentioned, and on irrigated sections of the prairie-and those areas are increasing. I suggest to the minister that he adopt a system somewhat analogous to that which is applied in connection with income tax, and that there be an exemption of, say fifteen bushels to the acre before the levy is applied.

It would be pretty
hard to keep track of that.

Well, then, cut it out
altogether, as someone has suggested. If that is not possible, why levy it on the low grades, why not levy on the top grades only? The hon. member for Wood Mountain has already half-advanced that argument. I have stressed
many times that there is a very large amount of low-grade grain grown in all of the provinces. When a farmer has even a large yield of low-grade grain, his money return is small and he would feel rather severely a one per cent levy. Perhaps the top three grades should meet this levy, but I still believe there ought to be a ten or fifteen bushel to the acre exemption to make the plan fair and equitable and ensure that only those who can afford to pay will pay.

I may say that all
the communications I have had from the west, particularly from farm organizations, are to the effect that this is one of the best features of the bill.
It is, definitely.

They say that in the
whole history of the organizations they have been advocating crop insurance and have insisted at all times that the farmer himself should make some payment toward it. I believe it would be a mistake to do away with this feature of the legislation. It establishes one of the main features of what will be in the future an insurance plan. I think all of those who have made a real study of the necessities of an insurance plan as applied to our farming in the west will agree we should at least assume that it is our responsibility as western farmers to pay one per cent to start off the scheme, at any rate in the first jrear, and as we go along we shall get experience in it and can adjust these matters to determine whether we want to pay on higher acreages more than we are paying here, or whether we want to go in the opposite direction and collect less and pay on lower acreages. These matters can be determined as we go along in the working of the legislation.

I have no objection to
insurance premiums. That is what I meant.

We are very much in favour of crop insurance, and we always have been. We advocate that there should be some form of equitable insurance applied to farming, not only that those in the drought areas should be cared for, but those in the other areas as well. I think it is generally conceded that the drought area of Saskatchewan, the southern part of Alberta, and a portion of Manitoba, is here to stay unless something is done in the form of irrigation, which possibly is impracticable in southern Saskatchewan, and I believe that the land which is commonly termed the drought area
3S3S
Prairie Farm Assistance

should be cut out entirely so far as this insurance scheme is concerned. So far as this levy goes, it should be applied only to those places which are reasonably assured of having a crop. But those portions in the south do not, so far as most of their area is concerned, have a crop at all, and this insurance plan is merely to take those people off relief. It is another form of relief; yet this is a national emergency, and it is something over which the people have no control. Drought is not a man-made affair. For that reason we contend that this drought area should be excluded from the insurance plan, and carried as a national responsibility.
That is what is provided for in the resolution.
You are making it carry itself.
Yes, you are making it carry itself from this one per cent tax.
No. The one per cent tax will carry only a percentage of the insurance end of it. That is a pure relief proposition provided for entirely out of the federal treasury.
A portion is from this one per cent.

No, because there will not be enough collected to contribute a portion from it. It is from five bushels an acre up to twelve bushels an 'acre, as it is in the legislation now. That is where the insurance feature comes in, the other being entirely a matter of assistance given to farmers.
That portion which the dominion will contribute is a loan put into this fund.
In effect, it is more than that.
There is no obligation to repay it.
There is an obligation to repay it if the dominion government asks them.
Only if the money comes in.
How much money do 3'ou think you will get this year?
One per cent means a great deal to these people. That drought area is something permanent; it is there to stay.
How do you know?

We are talking not from the point of view of a single farmer but from the point of view of the whole drought area, and even the Minister of Agriculture considers this drought area a permanent condition.
It is not permanent in the sense that they will not have any crop any year but in the sense that you may have three or four bad crops in succession.
They may get one crop in fifteen years as the farmers did in the southeastern part of Alberta.
You do not know what you are talking about.
I do, because I lived there, and I know that in the southeastern part of Alberta, round Youngstown, they have had one crop in fifteen years.
There is no one living there now.
We had twenty good years before that. I know, because I am familiar with the southeastern part of Saskatchewan. I have harvested more wheat there than the hon. gentleman has done.

As it happens, I was not talking about southeastern Saskatchewan; if the hon. member had been listening he would know that I was referring to the southeastern part of Alberta, round Youngstown. I intended to move an amendment, but I do not think I will at this time. However, I would ask the minister to consider putting this drought area outside the insurance scheme, and the rest of the people would have no objection to paying the one per cent and carrying their own insurance. The people in the western provinces have a legitimate objection to paying a levy for the purpose of raising a drought area out of relief, and that area should be excluded.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This type of discussion carries my mind back thirty years to the very first efforts that were made in western Canada to get the farmers there to agree to cooperate in matters of crop damage and insurance. We have here exactly a repetition of the same arguments: "Because we live in the north we have one type of damage and because you live in the south you have another, and therefore no means can be found of providing mutual assistance." I suggest that this is the most generous offer ever made by the people of Canada along the

Prairie Farm Assistance
lines of crop insurance, and the western farmer is simply asked to contribute a moiety of the whole cost, and only when he has it.
And then they kick.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: One per cent of the value of what he has when he has it. I still know the western farmers and get letters from many of them, and I know they regard this as a sound move in the right direction. It is not perfection; it is not something that will not have to be adjusted as the years go by, but it is a start on something which was begun thirty years ago in the west under great difficulties and subject to precisely the same arguments and disagreements that we are witnessing this afternoon. The people of Canada are standing behind this measure and asking the farmers of the west to contribute one per cent in value of the grain which they sell. If its value is low the contribution from the one per cent will be low; if it is high, as I hope it will be, then the contribution will be high; and very willing will the western farmers be to pay the one per cent out of a high price should they be fortunate enough to get a high price for their wheat. If we should be fortunate enough to have the returns that we have had in the past twenty years, then I can see the basis of a fund which will be standing there to help in days when calamity overtakes us.

From the
letters that I receive from my constituency I can assure the committee that the people are certainly in favour of crop insurance, but they wish to contribute their fair share to it. How can members from western Canada reason that we should not contribute our share? How can we with any sense of fairness ask the government to advance the price from 60 cents to 70 cents and from 70 cents to 80 cents, and then expect to exempt ourselves from contributing a small portion by way of crop insurance? The people in the constituency which I represent do not want that kind of legislation. I think the Minister of Finance will find that this measure meets the feelings of all reasonable farmers of western Canada.
While I do not think any farmers object to contributing, I point out that there are people who will have to contribute if they have a crop and yet may not get any benefit if they have no crop.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is always so.

Take, for
instance, hail insurance; that is worked on an individual basis.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is not worked on an individual basis.
I have to pay it everj year in my municipal taxes.
But a man may not have a bushel of crop and yet not come under the benefit of this measure.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He may not have a. bushel of crop and yet have to pay towards hail insurance for those who have. That is the law.
But here a man is bound to contribute but is not bound to get any return.
If he comes under the conditions of the bill he will get a return.

But there are many conditions and it is very easy for a man not to come under them. That is the only unfair aspect. If a man could be assured that in the event of crop failure he would get benefit, there would be no objection to contributing; but it is possible that he would have to contribute if he has a crop and, if he happens to have no crop, may be unable to fulfil the conditions, because of the price element or the area qualification or the price being above 80 cents, and so cannot draw benefit.
A man who pays fire insurance is very glad if he never gets anything back, but he knows that if his property is destroyed he will draw his insurance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Under the conditions set out in the policy.

But under
this bill it is quite possible that a man who contributes may find the conditions such, except for 1939, that he will not be able to draw one cent although he may have contributed for years. He may have contributed for ten years and yet, because the price is over 80 cents or the area in which he lives is not large enough, although he has no crop he cannot qualify. I suppose it cannot be done now, but I hope the department will work towards the idea of dealing with these people on an individual basis rather than by townships, that if a man has no crop he will be sure of some return if he is regularly contributing to this fund.
How much does the department expect to raise as a result of this one per cent levy?

It will depend entirely upon the price of grain and the amount for that year. Anyone can take the returns of
Prairie Farm Assistance

the years gone by and calculate what it would be in any particular year from the yield and value of our wheat. It is probably around S2.000.000 to $3,000,000. For the last year the payments from the fund would have been eight or nine times that amount.

What is the reason for the provision in subsection 7:
Notwithstanding the provisions of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That provision of the audit act requires that sums which are paid out of the consolidated revenue fund must be paid on the basis of a specific instrument of parliament; that is either an estimate or a statute calling for that specific sum, or, failing that, a warrant. Here we have a fund, and it is impossible to vote specific amounts out of it; therefore the provision to pay moneys out would contravene that specific section of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act.
I notice the licencee is responsible for making the reports and that sort of thing under subsections 4 and 5. Is any compensation or payment to be made for doing that?
No. They asked for compensation, but we suggested they should do without. They made the request but did not press it.
For collecting the sales tax the province pays a small percentage. This means a great deal of work. I wondered if the government had given the matter consideration.
It has been given consideration; they made a request but did not press it.

Do I understand this correctly, that in an area which qualifies under this clause, having less than five bushels to the acre, the money given is not taken from the revenue derived from the fund of one cent a bushel?

As a matter of fact it is; that is, they all pay in one per cent of the value of the grain that is delivered. But as a matter of fact there will probably be collected sufficient to pay only one-eighth or one-ninth of what was paid out last year for relief and the other matter too. And over a term of years it would work out that the obligation as to the amount paid where yields are under 
five bushels, that is what might be termed the relief end or assistance to people who have nothing at all, would, under this legislation, be assumed almost in its entirety if not in its entirety by the federal government. The moneys paid in by individuals, no matter what the size of their crop, will all be required, and additional amounts will be required in order to pay what might be termed the insurance end for those who have not complete crop failures.
From 1920 to 1928 would it have been possible to pay the compensation from the fund?
From 1922 to 1928, yes; 1920 and 1921 were not good years.

Section agreed to.
Section 7 agreed to.
On section 8-Award protected from attachment. Not assignable.
How would this affect a man operating a farm on a crop-share basis?

This section is intended to mean that every dollar of this money will go to the individual farmer and no one can take it from him. He can pay his grocery biil or other bills or buy groceries, but no one can garnishee or take this money from him.
If a mortgage company advanced seed they cannot collect it back out of this?
Not out of this money.

Section agreed to.
Section 9 agreed to.
On section 10-Officers, clerks and employees.

Will these
officers and employees who are to be appointed to carry on the administration of this measure come under the civil service commission?
No.
They will be temporary employees?
Yes.
Selected by the minister?

Yes, by the governor in council.

Canadian Wheat Board
Will their salaries or remuneration be paid out of the fund provided by the levy, or out of moneys voted by this parliament?
Nothing is to be paid out of the amount collected, except the insurance.
So that the salary or wages of every officer or employee would have to be passed as an estimate by this house before it could be paid?
Not necessarily.
Will these appointments be yearly or just temporary?

Quite a number will have to be temporary; they would only cover a month or two in the fall. Checking the acreages would probably be done earlier in the season, but checking the crop yields would be done in the fall.
Will they be provincial or federal appointments?
Federal.

Section agreed to.
On section 11-Offences.

I suppose one should not too closely scrutinize these bills to discover legal inaccuracies or ambiguities, because, I suppose, lawyers must live. It has even been suggested to me that there might have been method in the draftsman's madness. We all know what he had in his mind, but it is not expressed very clearly. It was Boileau, the great French literary critic, who wrote: Ce que Ton eongoit bien s'enonce clairement Et les mots pour le dire arrivent aisement.
Or, to translate roughly:
What you have in your mind clearly You can express clearly,
And the words to say it come easily.
I have drafted something which would perhaps cover the matter:
That section 11 be amended by striking out the word "who" in the third line thereof and all the words in paragraph (b) and substituting therefor the following words:
Whose information or return, furnished as required by regulation, is false;
And by adding the word "who" at the beginning of paragraph (c);
And by adding the word "such" before the word "false" and by striking out the words "required by regulation" in subsection 2 of said clause.
I so move.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
Section 12 agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall I report the bill.
What about the suggestion of the hon. member foi Rosthern?

It would be unlucky to call it clause 13, but I suggest that a clause be added as No. 12 (b), providing for publication. I think in a matter as important as this it would be well to provide for publication.
In the Canada Gazette?

Yes. I suggest that the subsection read:
All orders in council and all regulations made under the provisions of the act, or an abstract thereof disclosing their essential provisions, shall be published in the next following issue of the Canada Gazette.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Let that be subsection 2 of section 12.
I so move.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL

speechtext:
Hon. W. D. EULER (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved the second reading of Bill No. 63, to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act, 1935.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is customary upon second reading of a bill to have a pretty full discussion of the principle of it. I believe, however, it was pretty well understood when the complementary Bill No. 83, which was disposed of and passed this afternoon, was
Canadian Wheat Board

under discussion, that members of the house should be permitted to discuss the principle of Bill No. 63 as well. I think that was done quite fully, and while I have no intention of suggesting that debate or discussion on second reading should in any way be curtailed, it does occur to me that possibly since the principle has been discussed pretty well, the clauses might be discussed more fully in committee. That, however, is merely by the way.
I shall content myself, therefore, with stating very briefly the provisions of the bill. It speaks for itself and is perfectly clear, whether hon. members agree with it or not. The most important part of the bill deals with the removal of the power of the government, upon the recommendation of the wheat board, to fix an advanced payment, usually at the beginning of the crop season. That clause is replaced with one by which the bill itself fixes the advance price definitely at 70 cents a bushel, basis No. 1 northern Fort William. In other respects the bill is practically as it was originally. That is to say, the provisions are practically the same as they were before, with, of course, the participation clause remaining.
There are, however, two other clauses, one of which might be said to limit the application of the present wheat board act, and the other to broaden or extend it. The first one limits to 5,000 the number of bushels which may be sold by any one producer to the wheat board. The other provides for the extension of the application of the provisions of the bill to what is known as the eastern provinces.
I would add, in regard to the last clause, that in reading it again and discussing it with some hon. members there appears to be the possibility that its intent is not quite clear. Of course the intention is that the bill shall apply to the eastern provinces. As it reads at the present time it might appear that it is optional with the wheat board or the government as to whether or not it shall apply to eastern Canada. At the proper time, when the clause is under discussion, one of my colleagues will introduce a small amendment, so as to clarify the situation.

Mr. Speaker, the other day I pretty well outlined my point of view with reference to Bill No. 63 in the general discussion which took place on Bill No. 83. There are, however, one or two observations I should like to make with reference to Bill No. 63, because, after all, this and not Bill No. 83 is the bill which has aroused the ire of western Canada. While Bill No. 83 was brought in first, it was known

that most of us would agree with the general principle of crop insurance. Bill No. 63 is the bill to which we have really taken very strong exception. Speaking for the group with which I am associated, I would say that we are strenuously opposed to the clauses contained in Bill No. 63, with the exception of the new clause which provides that the benefits of the wheat board legislation shall be extended to the fanners of eastern Canada. Apart from that, we are opposed to the bill, in its entirety.
May I point out, first of all, that in its original form, prior to the bringing in of the bill now before us, the wheat board act would have permitted the wheat board, with the approval of the governor in council, to set a price. That was a much more satisfactory arrangement, by virtue of the fact that they could set a price the last week in July or some time in August, when crop possibilities could be gauged much more accurately than they can be gauged at this time of year.
In its original form, before being redrafted to the form in which it now stands, the bill proposed an initial price of 60 cents. Hon. members will realize that this was 27J cents less than the initial price paid by the wheat board in 1935, when the board first came into operation. Under pressure of public opinion throughout western Canada, which was exerted upon members of parliament and upon the government, this bill, along with Bill No. 83, was withdrawn. Therefore I say we object to this bill on these two grounds: first, on the basis of the limitation of 5.000 bushels. I pointed out the other day the whole tendency in western Canada, under strain of competition, owing to the fact that the price for primary commodities has been going down, and the price of commodities the farmers have to buy has been more or less stationary-with the exception that the price of farm machinery has been going up-is that farmers have been compelled to move into larger units of production. In a great many instances-I know many hon. members will have heard of such instances-a farmer has been forced out of business. Instead of a new man going on the farm, one neighbour will rent a quarter section, another neighbour will take another quarter section and the farm is more or less subdivided. Each farmer thus increases his own holdings. The result is they have more land to cultivate. They mechanize their

equipment and the result is a more efficient farm unit. As Professor Hope pointed out, the two-section unit is the most efficient unit of production. With this 5,000 bushel provision, farmers will be compelled to sell part of their wheat in competition with the wheat board, and they will not get the benefit of this legislation.
The second feature in this bill to which I object is the fixed price. In the first place, it is too low and, in the second place, it ought not to be set by statute. The minister gave a few cursory remarks to-day when introducing this bill, but as yet he has given no adequate explanation why the wheat board act could not have been allowed to continue to operate as it did in the past and the price be set in the fall by order in council. No adequate explanation has been given for that. This bill was brought down in April to set a price for a crop which will not be harvested until next August. I should like to draw attention once more to the submission of the western committee on markets and agricultural readjustment which was presented to the government and which advocated a continuing of the wheat board and a guaranteed minimum price of at least 80 cents a bushel for the 1939 wheat crop.

provision for it in the wheat board act and it is still called a fixed price. To quibble as to whether it is a fixed price or an initial price is merely attempting to get round the issue. I want to refer to this submission by the western conference because it is representative of a wide section of western Canada. It represents the opinions of some men who are associated politically with hon. members opposite and, therefore, it ought to carry a great deal of weight with the government when considering this matter. It reads:
Mr. Prime Minister and honourable ministers:
This delegation appears before you on behalf of the western committee on markets and agricultural readjustment. In this delegation are included accredited representatives of:
The United Farmers of Alberta, the United Farmers of Manitoba, the United Farmers of Canada (Saskatchewan section), the boards of trade of Regina, Saskatoon, Edmonton and Calgary, the Alberta wheat pool, Manitoba pool elevators, the Saskatchewan wheat pool, the North West Grain Dealers' Association, the United Grain Growers, the Alberta municipal association and the Manitoba government.
It is thus representative of those who are entitled to speak on behalf of the farmers of western Canada as well as of western business.
The original conference of which the presence of this delegation is the outcome was held in the city of Winnipeg on December 12th to 15th, 1938, inclusive. It was called by the government of Manitoba to consider the question of markets for western farm products, to discuss the situation of western agriculture and the disabilities which presently beset it, to assemble
the essential facts and to take such action by way of representation to constituted authority, continued study, recommendation, and self-help as might eventually be evolved, not only with respect to western agriculture, but also with regard to the general economy of Canada of which agriculture forms such a dominant part.
The conference was very largely attended, not only by producers, but also by organizations primarily interested in western agriculture, including representatives of both industry and business, not only from western Canada, but also from eastern Canada.
Universities cooperated by sending their professors and scientists. The deliberations were assisted and advanced by the experience and knowledge of several outstanding members of the dominion civil service and prominent officers of the United States department of agriculture. Assistance from all of these sources was greatly appreciated.
The proceedings of that conference have now been published, and we desire to file with you copies of these proceedings as representing a first-hand analysis of the western problem as it exists at the present time.
The contributions to the conference and the discussion that followed thereon were designed to crystallize the problem of western agriculture in the terms of ascertained facts.
The following legitimate deductions from the facts presented to the conference seem to be of especial significance and cogency.
I.	The prosperity of western Canada and to a large extent the prosperity of Canada depend upon the production of wheat and its sale at a reasonable price.
Without continued production of wheat on the present scale or on a scale approximate thereto and without exports to make such production possible, the west cannot continue to support its present population. We have other agriculture, and we have other industries, but they form part of an economic fabric, the strength of which depends mainly upon what happens to wheat. There is no other corresponding area and no other corresponding population in the world so dependent upon export trade in wheat.
There can be no other people so firmly determined as those of western Canada to maintain such a trade, as a matter of sheer necessity. Nor, since a quarter of the country's population is affected, is there any other country in the world so vitally concerned with the export wheat trade as is Canada.
The economic argument is strengthened by the facts of history. Professor Mackintosh, in discussing this question at the Winnipeg Conference, said:
"Confederation from the point of view of national economic development meant two things, union and definite expansion. Union meant a coordinating policy directed by a single government and not by the governments of four separate colonies; it meant financial strength and ability to enter the London money market, which was the source of capital necessary for the development of any new country; it meant a credit-worthy government.

Yes, I have already done so. It is from the submission to the government by the western committee on markets and agricultural readjustment.
Canadian Wheat Board

They are here quoting from Professor Mackintosh's statement to the Winnipeg conference on wheat marketing problems. To continue with the brief:
We submit that the great national purposes to be served as a result of confederation and its immediate objective, namely, the development of western Canada, has not been disappointing to the dominion as a whole; that great results have been forthcoming, not only in terms of a period of well-being in the Canadian west, but in terms of a consequent expansion in other parts of Canada and the building up of the nation as we understand it to-day. We further submit that the national objective involved in the development of western Canada continued to be a great driving force in Canadian development up until 1930. Even during the depression period through Which we are passing the west has contributed substantially to federal revenues under a tariff which between 1930 and 1935 was the highest in Canadian history.
2.	The tariff, which was greatly increased in the early stages of the depression, while constituting emergency relief for eastern Canada, bore heavily upon western Canada. Eastern reciprocity in sharing the burden of an emergency western wheat crisis is only the fulfilment of an obligation that has been long outstanding.
3.	Western Canada's production of wheat is generally more than three times as much per year as Canada herself requires. We must therefore find an external market for two-thirds or more of our production.
4.	As a result of declining world prices the 1938 crop, which was more than twice as large as the 1937 crop, would bring at recent market prices some 30 million dollars less than the 1937 crop.
5.	During the seven years from 1931 to 1937 there was a decline of $2,540,000,000 in the gross value of agricultural production in the prairie provinces as compared with the corresponding value from 1924 to 1930, of which decline something more than half was accounted for by lower prices. Consequent reduction in income has_ not only brought depression in the west, but is also one of the most important causes of depression experienced in other parts of Canada preventing a return to full employment in recent years.
6.	The wheat industry of western Canada, which finds itself caught in the current of economic nationalism, subsidized export competition and strangling international political forces over which our producers have no control, is entitled as an industry to receive from the nation as a whole emergency price assistance.
7.	Assistance actually rendered to the wheat industry^ has been small, especially if it is considered in relation to the extent and duration of the depressed period through which the industry has passed, in relation to the assistance rendered to growers in other exporting countries and in importing countries during the comparable period, and in relation to the great wealth it has produced for Canada. Only for the 1938 crop are actions by the dominion government likely to involve a relatively large cost. Risks were assumed by the dominion government in previous years, but the ultimate liability was practically negligible. Considerable sums have been spent for relief to farmers who suffered total or partial crop failure. For

this the dominion government deserves the fullest commendation. While appreciating to the full the value of such assistance to those in need, we submit that it differs from protection to the wheat industry as such and that it would have been necessary even if prices had remained at remunerative levels throughout the whole of the period under review.
8.	Because the western wheat farmer has had to bear the heavy burden of low prices and poor yields during all the depression period, his financial reserves have been largely eliminated and the disparity between his debts and the income from which these debts can be carried greatly widened. Western debt can only be serviced and amortized in terms of the volume and price of wheat.
9.	The competitive position of the wheat exporting countries is not only determined by their efficiency in the production and marketing of wheat, but at the present time also bv the varying degree of state assistance which enables the industry in each country to maintain its relative position.
10.	While wheat importing countries have striven to increase their own production of wheat, this factor has been of minor importance compared with the effects of trade restrictions imposed largely as defence measures, military or financial. Thus while wheat prices at Liverpool have declined to levels approaching the lowest on record, and while our northern wheat is selling at 60 cents per bushel at Fort William, the consumers of wheat in some of the formerly large wheat importing countries of continental Europe are actually paying as high or higher than $2 per bushel for wheat used in their breadstuffs. Even in the United Kingdom, which is now a free market for imported wheat, the government has established a fixed price of about $1.30 per bushel for millable homegrown wheat. Consequently, through the intervention of governments, producers in importing countries are protected from the effects of low international prices and consumers are prevented from enjoying the benefits of cheap bread. Under prevailing conditions low international prices are largely ineffective in bringing about stimulation in world consumption of wheat or in bringing about an increase in world trade.
_ 11. With the wheat industry playing such an important part in the domestic economies of Canada, the United States, the Argentine and Australia, it was inevitable that an effort should be made to protect their wheat growers. The United States has, for many years, been extending direct assistance to wheat farmers under the Agricultural Adjustment Act and other legislation, assistance which involves many hundreds of millions of dollars. In the present crop year that country reinforced price supporting measures by paying an export subsidy in an effort to retain a share of world markets. The Australian government, after experimenting with various forms of assistance, involving, according to a tabulation in the royal grain inquiry commission, payments of 14 million pounds during the years 1931-32 to 1935-36, is this year imposing a special tax on domestically consumed flour in order to assist wheat growers. The Argentine government is this year following its established practice of paying a minimum price to growers, a price which is at present above the world market level. In addition, both the Argentine and Australia have adopted

Canadian Wheat Board
monetary policies which have facilitated exports and at the same time have improved the relative position of their producers within their domestic economies. It is apparent from what has been done in this direction that none of the large wheat exporting countries has been prepared to see its internal economy and its external position determined by whatever prices may prevail in world markets.
12.	The resultant forces of high production, low consumption and low prices combined in their impact upon western Canada in 1938. A major economic disaster was only averted by the prompt action of the dominion government, through the Canadian wheat board in fixing a guaranteed price of 80 cents basis One Northern in store Fort William. The same forces now threaten the outlook for 1939.
13.	The Canadian economy 'has, to a very large extent, been built around its export industries, chief among which has been the wheat industry. For many years now Canada's exports of wheat, wheat flour, and other milled products, have constituted from 20 to 38 per cent of Canadian export trade. The wheat industry has established very substantial foreign credits which have been an essential factor in the service of the country's external debt, and in the provision of new capital in the maintenance of a rapidly growing country. It is in the interests of the nation as a whole, with due consideration to Canada's obligations abroad, to make a major effort to retain the wheat industry which means the continuance of assistance during abnormal conditions and effective measures to regain lost markets and to establish new ones.
14.	An 80-cent price, which is equivalent this year to a farm price of about 57 cents for average grades, will not permit payment of debt on ,the average farm except in cases of better than average yields, or at the expense of a serious reduction in standards of living in western farm homes, but it will help to carry the wheat farmer and the wheat industry through a crisis.
15.	The development of the prairie provinces was accompanied by the investment of large sums of money. In the development of the west, capital was provided not only from eastern Canada, but from many countries, including the United States, the United Kingdom, Holland, Belgium and France. A breakdown in the financial structure o>f western Canada, which must inevitably follow another period of low prices for wheat, would have far-reaching effects upon the credit of the Canadian nation as a whole. If the nation wishes to maintain a satisfactory credit position it must do its courageous part in meeting the western emergency.
16.	The financial results of protection for
the western wheat industry in 1938 should not be considered only from the viewpoint of first cost to the dominion treasury. The money go provided is not lost to the people of Canada, but is distributed mainly:	(a) In additional
purchases of eastern goods and the increase of inwai-d freights.
(b)	In the payment of taxes and the reduction of federal assistance that would otherwise have inevitably been necessary for relief purposes.
(c)	In payment of debt.
I might point out here that a number of implement companies' representatives went out last fall and collected for farm machinery a great deal of money which they would not have been able to collect if the farmer had not received this guaranteed minimum price of 80 cents last year.
17.	The federal system of administration in Canada and the regional nature of the Canadian economy have involved transfers of income as between different economic groups and as between different regions.
As a consequence of the Canadian tariff structure the west for many years now has been transferring a portion of its income to the central provinces of Canada, a transfer of income which over a long period of time amounts to many hundreds of millions of dollars. The conditions now existing in respect to the wheat industry fully justify the recognition of the principle of compensation to agriculture as a partial offset for the bonuses agriculture pays to the secondary industries through the tariff.
Incidentally it may be pointed out that at the very inception of the depression an abnormal transfer of income was made to the secondary industries of this country through the revisions of the tariff in 1930 and amendments to the Customs Act. This action, taken at a time when the wheat industry was involved in a serious crisis, reduced competition in the domestic market by making importation into Canada exceedingly difficult, and resulted in the maintenance of a relatively high price structure for manufactured goods sold in the domestic market. This emergency action taken in 1930 was. in effect, an additional subsidy to the secondary industries of this country, a subsidy which was largely paid for by the primary industries even though they themselves were in economic difficulty.
