I do not want to stop now to argue the matter, but I think the point the committee are here endeavouring to make is that, by virtue of this tariff protection, the element of competition had been removed, and that, while there may have been steps taken to keep prices from going up, that element of competition was not present which might have brought prices down when other prices were coming down. There are just three more reasons given by them:
18.	It is impossible for the wheat industry to bear the burden of high tariff costs and low wheat prices at the same time. . . .
19.	Special consideration has not infrequently been given to different groups in Canada. For example, monetary policy during the depression protected creditor interests, and fiscal policy has consistently protected secondary industries.

Canadian Wheat Board

20.	The wheat industry of the prairie provinces, measured on the basis of the numbers of people concerned, in terms of wealth produced, and in terms of its effect on internal and external trade in Canada, reveals itself as being of such importance that it is essential for the dominion to stand behind it.
21.	With due regard to the degree of diversification which has taken place in western agriculture, it is in the national interest to preserve the present balance in farm production as between the various regions^ in Canada. Agriculture in Canada reached its most prosperous stage when the west was fulfilling its primary function of producing wheat for export. As long as this situation continued the west gave the agricultural producers of other parts of Canada a fair opportunity to carry on their industry without undue competition from the prairie provinces. In fact it may be said that the interests of the prairie provinces in the export market rather than in the domestic market permitted producers in other parts of Canada to enjoy relatively prosperous markets internally.
Any substantial or violent change in western agriculture at this time will adversely affect the balance of agriculture in Canada and the prosperity of eastern agriculture.
We would like to refer to the 80 cents guaranteed price paid in respect to the 1938 crop. After allowing for transportation, handling costs, and grades lower than No. 1 Northern, the western farmer is receiving an average of about 57 cents per bushel on the farm. Were it not for the fixed price this year western farmers would be receiving about 37 cents a bushel for their wheat, farm basis.
It is interesting to note that Ontario farmers received about 58 cents a bushel for their wheat in the local markets, or about the same price that the western farmer is receiving under the 80 cent guarantee. We would like to call your attention to the fact that prices for other grains are much higher in Ontario than in the prairie provinces. For instance, oats are worth 29 cents per bushel in Ontario and 16 cents a bushel in Saskatchewan. Barley is worth 41 cents per bushel in Ontario and 22 cents per bushel in Saskatchewan. Fall rye is worth 44 cents per bushel in Ontario and 25 cents a bushel in Saskatchewan. Thus, under the 80 cent guaranteed price on wheat, the western farmer is receiving no more than the eastern farmer, and he receives only about one-half the price that the eastern farmer is receiving for oats, barley and rye. The foregoing farm prices are averages for the 1938-39 crop year as published by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics.
The committee then go on to outline their resolutions, which I cannot take time to read now. They outline the meeting which they had in Regina on January 21, when they drew up a resolution which concludes in this way:
By way of general direction to its sub-committee, this committee offers for its guidance, its unanimous opinion that the dominion government should be requested to extend to the western wheat growers in respect of the wheat to be grown in the crop year 1939-40 at least the protection given in the crop year 1938-39.
[Mr. T. C. Douglas.1
Then they go on to tell of the meeting they had in Saskatoon on February 14, when again they passed a resolution asking for the continuation of the wheat board and for a fixed price of not less than 80 cents, and it was arranged to present this brief to the government-which they did. In their report they then proceed to draw to the attention of the government the value of the wheat board and the importance of retaining it as a permanent marketing agency, and they point out what they regard as an important fact, namely, that the marketing of wheat ought not to be confused with relief measures and that a relief measure such as passed through this house to-day, Bill No. 83, cannot possibly be accepted as a substitute for a guaranteed minimum price of 80 cents. They submit that you are dealing with two classes of people and that a relief measure such as the acreage bonus scheme has to do with people who have no crop, whereas the Canadian Wheat Board Act affects people who have a crop and who desire to market it at a reasonable price. They insist that these two points of view should be kept separate and distinct, should be dealt with separately and distinctly, and that we should not try to do what has been done and what, I am afraid, will continue to be done; that is, that you should not lump the two together and say we cannot have the one without the other.
There is nothing at all that would have made it impossible for the government to accept the suggestion of this committee and fix the initial price in the wheat board act at 80 cents and at the same time have the acreage bonus scheme. Since this house has passed the acreage bonus scheme, there is nothing to prevent the government from altering this bill or sending it to the committee on agriculture where it could be gone into thoroughly and, if it were thought wise, recommendation could be made to the house that the price be raised to 80 cents.
No member of the house in voting for this bill can escape his responsibility merely by saying that he had to accept it in order to get the acreage bonus scheme, because the two are separate and distinct bills. You can vote for the one without voting for the other. They are not interwoven. We in this comer were prepared to support the acreage bonus scheme although we thought that there should be changes in it, and we did support it in principle. We will not support this bill, because we are convinced first of all that the restriction of 5,000 bushels to each producer is a discrimination against the most efficient producers on the prairies.

Canadian Wheat Board
I am quite willing to concede that it would not be wise to let people sell all their wheat to the wheat board; it might be necessary to put it on a graduated scale. But certainly there should not be a fixed limit of 5,000 bushels which would penalize the people on the best farms round the Regina plains, Rose-town-Biggar, the Soo line, Kindersley and Elrose, which are among the most efficient producers in Saskatchewan. For that reason we object to the bill and we hope that the minister will seriously reconsider it. We object to the price of 70 cents, which is totally inadequate to meet the situation, and we do not feel that the government can escape the condemnation of the farmers of western Canada by trying to get this bill through the house by virtue of the good graces of the acreage bonus scheme.
Mr. CHARLES E. FERLAND (Joliette-
L'Assomption-Montcalm) (Translation): Mr. Chairman, the bill now before us is entitled "An Act to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act, 1935." Its purpose is to amend" the act whereby the Bennett government instituted that wheat board and granted special privileges to Canadian wheat growers.
I was very much surprised, during this debate and the discussion on bill 83, to hear a great number of hon. members from the west criticize this government's agricultural legislation and state their intention of voting against the relief measures introduced with a view to helping wheat growers. If we are to believe the hon. member who has just resumed his seat, the sole problem which must be solved in this country is the wheat problem, and it covers the entire field of agriculture. Problems that are far more important than wheat growing are involved in the agricultural industry and the wheat problem does not, by any means, constitute the whole agricultural problem. It is nevertheless considered as an all-important one by every great wheat producing country. The European nations, the United States, Argentina and Canada, all of which are growing wheat, recognize that wheat is essentially a basic commodity and a most important one. That is why those countries have enacted legislation granting special privileges to wheat growers.
It was under the Bennett administration that our country adopted a wheat policy. The Bennett government first paid a bonus on wheat after which they introduced, in 1935, that act whereby a price was set on wheat and a Canadian Wheat Board was instituted. A reference to what the Bennett government did for agriculture will show that they endeavoured to pass three acts of the utmost 71492-2421
importance. The first was the Marketing Act which was passed by this House notwithstanding the objections of the Liberals who were of the opinion that such an act could not be passed under our constitution; that act was declared by our courts to be ultra vires. The second important piece of legislation respecting the farmers of Canada was the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. Through it, approximately 42,000 farmers settled debts amounting to over $200,000,000. As a result, the farmers' indebtedness has been reduced by about $80,000,000, of which $5,500,000 alone represent interests to date. Statistics are not complete in that respect, but I have been able to secure that information from the officer who is administering the act. Consequently, under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act passed by the Bennett administration, the farmers' creditors, who were mostly small rural moneylenders, lost $80,000,000 or contributed this amount toward alleviating the distress of these farmers, and this, without any governmental assistance whatever. Lastly, the Bennett government adopted the Wheat Board Act. I might also mention the legislation fathered by the Liberal government, which is designed to assist all farmers in general, and not solely those who produce wheat, namely, the Canadian Farm Loan Act.
According to the latest figures, the government has loaned to dale, under this Act, approximately $39,000,000, of which almost $11,000,000 is in the province of Quebec alone. Why did the province of Quebec thus obtain $11,000,000, while the other provinces received much smaller amounts? It is due to the fact that a measure adopted by the Taschereau government enabled the farmers to obtain farm loans from the both governments at an interest rate of 3 per cent. However, there is one recommendation I would like to make in this regard. Experience has revealed during the last few years, that it was possible profitably to administer the Canadian Farm Loan Act in the province of Quebec-there is more difficulty to be encountered elsewhere, for it seems to me that the western farmers carry a much greater burden of debt than those in the east.
The Canadian Farm Loan Act allows farmers to borrow up to 50 per cent of the value of their land on a first mortgage, and an additional 10 per cent, that is up to 60 per cent on a second mortgage, the maximum loan obtainable being set at $6,000. In the province of Quebec, it would be much easier and much more practical to administer this Act in a broad-minded manner, in a freer and more generous way, if the officials who
Canadian Wheat Board

are charged with its administration paid more attention to the spirit rather than to the letter of the law. Notwithstanding the great difficulties with which prospective borrowers are faced, they have succeeded in obtaining, under the federal legislation, almost SI 1,000,000. I would ask the higher officials in Ottawa, those whose duty it is to give out the necessary instructions with regard to the interpretation of this Act, to see that it is administered according to the spirit that prompted its introduction, and effectively to grant loans equivalent to 50 per cent of the value of the land on a first mortgage, and to 10 per cent on a second mortgage.
In the report published for the year ending March 31, 1938, I notice that the federal government has granted, under the Canadian Farm Loan Act, advances in the amount of $34,000,000 approximately, and that these loans are secured by mortgages valued at $106,000,000, so that the security obtained is at least two thirds greater than the amount advanced. Were the Act administered in a more liberal and equitable manner, our farmers would be able to borrow an amount equal at least to 50 per cent of the value of their lands, whereas in reality they have only received about one third. We could loan at least four or five millions more every year in Quebec alone.
The administration of this Act has not been very expensive. Although the government was authorized to loan $90,000,000 only $39,000,000 has been advanced under the provisions of the Act. This sum of $90,000,000 consists of $40,000,000 worth of Farm Loan Board bonds which the hon. Minister of Finance may hold as security against advances, in addition to other debentures valued at $50,000,000 which the board may place on the market and which are guaranteed by the government. Since these bonds bear interest at the rate of 3i per cent, their purchase by the public would offer no difficulty, and the government could thus loan considerable amounts without its costing the federal treasury very much. I am not at all advocating the granting of advances to farmers without demanding repayment. We are all aware of the fact that whatever happens, repayment is always effected through taxation, but I am in favour of any practical legislation by means of which the federal government can accelerate the circulation of money, distribute it in every part of the country, and then recover this money without the aid of further taxation.
To my mind, the present measure with respect to wheat is a very liberal one for the Western farmers. The honourable member for Prescott (Mr. Bertrand) stated the other day

that the dairy industry remains more important than the wheat industry, and he urged, as he and a great many other hon. members from the eastern provinces have so often done during this session, that all possible assistance be granted to the butter and cheese industry.
The government is to be congratulated on having, while continuing the Conservative policy of assisting the wheat growers, listened to our representations and placed on the statute book of the country for the first time substantial measures intended to aid the dairy industry by bringing about a raise in the price of this product, which at present is below 25 cents a pound. Farmers and cooperative societies have written to us and forwarded resolutions asking that the price of butter be raised to 25 cents at least.
Some encouragement has been given to the production of cheese. Large quantities of cheese can easily be shipped to England, whereas it is practically impossible to export any butter to that market. This substantial encouragement to the production of cheese will serve to reduce the production of butter, as our farmers will go in more for cheesemaking. I have already received from my constituency applications for some of the assistance which the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has placed at the disposal of the cheese industry. Western members who criticize the government in spite of the liberal, generous and very special legislation introduced On behalf of their people, do not seem to understand that the farmers of eastern Canada have problems of their own and indeed very serious ones. Operating in industrialized provinces where nearly one third of the population live in the cities and towns, they have to bear the burden to a certain extent of a protective tariff intended to make it possible for our manufacturing establishments to absorb the labour of the cities and create a sufficient market for the products of the eastern farms.
I have another suggestion to offer to the government in connection with this agricultural measure. The hon. member who has just taken his seat complained that the eastern farmers obtain a much higher price for their grain than the farmers of the prairies and he saw injustice in that situation. Therein lies an excellent opportunity for the government to help both the western grain grower and the eastern farmer interested in the dairy industry and in cattle, hog and chicken raising, by finding a way to distribute in the eastern provinces a certain amount of western grain at the prices prevailing in the west. The government would thus help the western

Canadian Wheat Board
grain growers to dispose of their crop while assisting the eastern farmers to purchase grain and grain products at reasonable prices instead of the exorbitant prices which they frequently have to pay now.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I appeal to hon. members from the west who so frequently make unreasonable demands, who show themselves so uncompromising, who seem to forget that the east has problems of its own, to show as much generosity towards the east as the east shows towards the west. I hope the government will give substantial assistance to the producers of the east, particularly the producers of butter and cheese, and in the near future, as I have just suggested and as it has been suggested by others outside the house, cause western grain to be distributed in the eastern provinces at the prices prevailing in the west.

It is our considered judgment that western Canada is facing the gravest crisis in its history. a fact which is not perhaps fully appreciated by many members of the house. Conditions in western Canada to-day exist probably nowhere else in the world. We are a long way from our markets; we have high freight rates and other problems to face, and the greatest problem facing the wheat grower of western Canada to-day is to get a sufficient price for his product to afford a decent livelihood for himself and those dependent upon him.

bushels at the advance price. A third principle of the bill extends the operation of the measure to eastern Canada. The inclusion of eastern Canada is entirely commendable. This bill should be considered with Bill No. 83, which the house passed this afternoon. I do not propose to discuss that feature at this time, except to point out that this bill provides for one thing in addition to what the other bill provided for. The two bills are complementary to each other.
I confess that there are in this bill some things which I should have liked to be a little different. I do not mind admitting that I regard the 5,000 bushel limitation as too low. It seems to me that a man who produces
5,000	bushels or more is penalized by having the one per cent deduction taken from his wheat for the benefit of less fortunate farmers. He is not likely to benefit much from the crop insurance scheme. Also the provision may be difficult to administer. I believe that if the amount were raised to a higher level the administrative difficulty would be materially lessened. In most communities nearly everyone knows the farmers who have more than eight or ten thousand bushels of wheat, so that the possibility of abuse, if a higher amount were allowed, would not be nearly so great as I fear it may be under the legislation as it stands.
I hope, too, that careful consideration will be given in this connection to what may be called the family farmer. We have in western Canada a situation where the father of the family is remaining on the farm with several sons. They have probably extended their farm operations to secure land which at some time will be available for each of these boys. Surely those people are entitled to be classed as farmers individually. I hope that these matters will be considered when the bill is before us in committee.
There are two or three things I should like to point out not so much with respect to the legislation as to the general picture of the wheat situation. Some of the figures I propose to mention have been quoted before, but for my purpose to-night I should like to quote them again because I think they will be found helpful in considering this all-important matter.
It is estimated that by next July we shall have a world cariy-over of 1,100,000,000 bushels of wheat. The world trade in wheat for the past two years has been between 540 and 560 million bushels. Consequently it will be seen that we have a world carry-over equal to almost two years' world trade in wheat without adding to it. That is based on the

world trade of the last few years. In addition, to that, we are likely to have a Canadian carry-over of probably 100 to 125 million bushels. This year's wheat marketing policy is likely to cost the taxpayers of Canada anywhere from 30 million to 50 million dollars. Further, notwithstanding the payment of money to assist wheat producers, we have had to spend another 12 million dollars in actual farm relief in the wheat growing areas of western Canada. I do not wish to delay the house, but I should like to quote a comment which has been made in another country respecting this feature as it affects Canada. This quotation is taken from Foreign Agriculture, a publication of the United States department of agriculture. Referring to the wheat situation in Canada, it says this, in part:
If exports this season reach the usual level of about 200,000,000 bushels, the cost to the Canadian government-
That is, under the present wheat policy.
-for exports alone will be approximately $40,000,000.
It goes on to say:
The Canadian price scheme for wheat does not impose any immediate burden on domestic consumers, since no attempt is made by the board to keep prices to domestic millers at levels higher than the prices secured for export wheat. The fact is, however, that losses incurred by the board must some time be met out of
Fublic funds, unless the price of wheat in the uture goes so high as to offset the board's losses. The situation is focusing Canadian official and public attention upon proposals to end the fixed-price system, although at present no substitute plan for wheat has been approved. The costs incurred to date represent a considerable burden for the Canadian population of about 12,000,000 people.
This publication is dealing with the situation in different countries, and that is what it has to say with respect to the Canadian situation.
The system under which we operated in the past year, that of paying a guaranteed advance price of 80 cents a bushel worked to the advantage of those who had a good crop, and did little or nothing for those who were unfortunate enough to have a poor crop or a low-yielding crop or no crop at all. In that sense it acted exactly as did the application of the five cents a bushel bonus proposed by the previous government. So that, in spite of what we may say with regard to it, there are bound to be inequalities in the actual carrying out of the scheme. It is admitted that it is an easy scheme to administer, that it produces very few difficulties in operation, that the system for it to function under is already made; but inequalities are bound to develop within it.
For example, this year-there is no gainsaying it-the government stands to pay roughly about twenty cents a bushel on each fMr. Weir.]
bushel of wheat marketed. Thus it will be appreciated that the man with a good crop is getting from the government a considerable payment which he may not have required. The man with thirty bushels to the acre will secure this year from the government a contribution of about S6 an acre. Others, on the other hand, have secured little or nothing. The inequalities to which I refer have been met to a certain extent by the second piece of legislation introduced at this session providing for a crop insurance scheme. In addition to that, under this legislation we have continued the participation certificate, which means that the 70 cent price as announced in the wheat board act is an advance price, so that if the price of wheat should go higher than 70 cents then the farmer will have an opportunity to take advantage of that advance. Moreover, no restrictions were placed on the farmer with regard to his deliveries or the amount of wheat the board might accept from him, until this year when we introduced the 5.000 bushel limitation.
Throughout this whole discussion on the wheat marketing legislation references are being constantly made to the demands by way of petition and otherwise that have come from western Canada for an advance price of 80 cents. These demands represent naturally the feeling of those who are particularly interested. In some instances they have been urged; but in others, particularly in the letters received from private individuals, there is evidence of a sincere and full appreciation of the condition in western Canada. So far as these petitions are concerned, I am bound to say that if the government is going to be forced to direct its policy upon the basis of such petitions as it may receive, then I do not know why it should continue to carry on as a government. After all, other sections of Canada can make representations by way of petition or otherwise-

I believe this government has recognized that fact, and realized the position of the western provinces, and accordingly it has moved in the direction of remedying these conditions. I refer to the Canada-United States-United Kingdom trade agreement as a long step in the right direction towards that alleviation, as is also the measure introduced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) last Saturday when he introduced the bill with regard to the mortgage discount bank. The information I am about to give to the house has been secured largely from the Department of Trade and Commer Monthly Review of the Wheat Situation and from the Foreign Exchange magazine of the United States department of agriculture as well as from our own bureau of statistics. I have compiled it in a way that will be more presentable to the house.
I will deal first with the Argentine. A minimum price for wheat was set in the Argentine on November 15, 1938, by presidential decree based upon legislation passed in September, 1938. The growers receive from the current crop seven pesos per quarts], equivalent to 59J cents a bushel for 62i pound wheat, delivered at Buenos Aires. Minimum prices for lower grades were set at appropriate spreads. The national grain board purchase wheat from growers on this basis and in turn resell it to exporters at competitive market prices. Losses incurred will be met by revenues from the operations of the exchange control board. Mr. Speaker, on the second reading of this bill I wish to address you for a few moments concerning some features to which references have not been made by other hon. members. The purpose of the amending bill is to limit the quantity of wheat the board may purchase from one producer. The words are:

Provided further that the hoard shall not purchase from any one producer more than five thousand bushels of wheat produced in any crop year.
I can remember the attitude taken by hon. members opposite about the time the pools began to operate. They opposed vigorously in the house the proposal I had advocated for some years, that there should be a wheat board to regulate operations in wheat, to market it and to ship the exportable surplus. They opposed regulations such as may be imposed upon railways, telephone companies and express companies in Canada by federal regulatory bodies. Such regulations were ridiculed in the house. After persuading one of the great newspapers to spend a great deal of money investigating this entire grain trade proposal I was told I was proposing a system of paternalism, when I supported the principle then of such a proposed wheat board, whereby it would be given wide grain functions.
Under this -measure the board will be reduced, so far as its functions are concerned. It is going to be tied down to a certain automatic rule, and will simply be reduced to the capacity of office boys, stenographers and all that sort of thing. I can remember when also aid came in opposition from Sir Henry Thornton who wanted to bring a million more wheat growers to the Northwest Territories and the Peace River district. We can realize what over-production of grain that would have involved. The grain industry would have been ruined' and wheat would have gone down to 50 cents a bushel.
In connection with this matter, I shall quote two or three observations which I made on a former occasion:
I know this proposal will be met with the shout of "paternalism." I would sooner have the paternalism of a protectionist government than the paternalism of the Winnipeg Grain Exchange and its allies, and the paternalism of a free trade that robs the growers of the best wheat in the world out of $25,000,000 per annum in the price of wheat, and puts that $25,000,000 into the pockets of the Americans who handle that wheat. We will have to have more paternalism in the management of this country's resources and the promotion of this country's welfare.
I believe those words were prophetic, because, after all is said and done, there should be no east or west or north or south in this question. The wheat growers and their great natural industry must be considered throughout the country as a whole. If the industry is a success, the banks and railways will benefit, as will the people in the east and west alike. The whole dominion will be benefited. It is of the utmost importance that we should not do anything here to-night which would weaken the position of that great basic industry,
{Mr. Church.]
an industry which has been the safety valve for business in Canada, both before and after confederation.
There are some features of the bill I do not like. It ignores the evidence taken in 1935 with respect to the grain act. My late leader created the grain board because it would be beneficial to the grain industry. He practically wanted to nationalize its scope and operations to aid the grower. If I can go by what I hear in the house and what I read outside the house, the wheat industry must be in a bad way to-day on the prairies. I think it is the duty of every good citizen to take a keen interest in the question and help it by wise precautions. I would not have taken part in this debate had it not been for the fact that people from Ontario pioneered in the prairie provinces and some of us are said not to be friendly in the matter. We were and are pioneers. I well remember, when I was five or six years of age, the great growth of that industry, and the movement connected with the sale of lots in what were known as Portage la Prairie lands. Thousands of people from Ontario went to the west then and pioneered in the wheat industry. For that reason I have always had a keen interest in it and its success has appealed to my fancy and imagination. I have watched the suffering that has taken place on the prairies, and I hope nothing will be said which would interfere with proper relief being given to that part of the country, and other sections, where want is for all the people all of the time.
The production of wheat is the most imperial and national industry Canada has, and one of the greatest the world has ever witnessed. It depends for its success on the British market very largely, and, for that reason, in view of what was said there yesterday by the Secretary of State for War, in the British House of Commons, namely, that the people of Britain must now be ready and sleep on their haversacks, I cannot understand why more extensive measures are not taken by the government. As I said last year, great storage reservoirs erected by Canada should have been created in the old country to take care of our exportable surplus. The carryover of last year and this year could have been taken over to Great Britain by this government and stored there in advance of the world's crisis. If we had had the vision to move that crop, the carry-over of last year and this year could have been stored in the old country.
The present bill narrows the scope of the whole wheat board. The marketing of grain is quite properly under the Minister of Trade

Canadian Wheat Board
and Commerce (Mr. Euler). After all is said and done, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is engaged with technical matters concerning agriculture, aid to farmers, aid to the poor grain growers who have been suffering and who have always been the victims of the middleman. There is a duplication in the provinces of the work of the Department of Agriculture. The function of the Department of Trade and Commerce is to advance our surplus overseas, market our crops, eliminate the middleman and get the best price for our wheat in the markets of the world, so that the poor grain grower who has suffered so much may receive some direct benefit, and his share of the profits with the middleman eliminated.
I cannot understand why the government of the day has not accepted' the suggestion which was made by Hon. H. A. Wallace, the very able federal secretary of the department of agriculture in the United States. He conferred once or twice with the former Prime Minister and Mr. McFarland, and this year again proposed that the two countries, Canada and the United States, should make a survey, act together and consider the possibility of joint action with regard to dividing the important overseas markets as am emergency measure for the joint orderly marketing of wheat on this continent. This marketing could have been carried on so that the two countries which are so closely related would not suffer. I cannot understand why the wheat board or the government did not accept this proposal, as the government of this country abrogated the six cent preference on wheat of the Ottawa agreements, which would have done so much to eliminate the carry-over of last year, the carry-over of this year and the carry-over of future years. That was a steady market in Britain for our wheat, not a market that was here to-day and away to-morrow. That preference carried with it the stipulation that the grain must be shipped in British ships. I cannot understand why that was not continued, and I should like to see all the papers in connection with that matter laid on the table of the house. I should like to know if the British government suggested this. Two free traders, Right Hon. Ramsay MacDonald and Oliver Stanley represented that government in negotiating the United States treaty with Great Britain. I should like to know if the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Trade and Commerce have received any correspondence from them or the United States. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) who spoke in the debate is the only Conservative from the prairies. Hon. gentlemen opposite after being free traders and wearing a coat of
many colours, are now adopting a policy of protection all along the line in the way of bonuses, stabilization funds, subsidies and all that kind of thing, which the wheat board should be carrying out.
I should like to know if the department or the minister has had any correspondence in connection with the handling of grain in the old country. The importing countries have reduced their imports by 20 per cent. Germany, France and Italy are growing that much for their own home markets. When we have such a large exportable surplus, how does it come about that Great Britain enters into an agreement with the United States, which has been produced in the British house and which has received some discussion in Washington, whereby Britain is to take 100,000,000 bushels of the exportable surplus of the United States in exchange for rubber and tin. That is about half our carry-over. Where are we going to find a market? The wheat board cannot find markets. Some of our markets are gone beyond recall forever. As I said in connection with the wheat board bill this year, regarding the United States treaty once this preference is gone the United Kingdom will have to make other arrangements. These other arrangements have now been made with the United States by Britain for 100,000,000 bushels. We are the losers.
I cannot understand why the wheat board and the government have not made any move also to reconvene the world's international advisory committee and attempt to negotiate an agreement with the major importing countries which have reduced our exports by 22 per cent. I have directed the attention of the house to the statement which was made in the British house in connection with the grain trade and Canada's exportable surplus. We must remember that we are in an emergency. Great Britain imports 90 per cent of her food and 97 per cent of her raw materials. Where is that food to come from? Mostly from the dominions. During 1919 Great Britain was almost starved out by the submarines which sunk our shipping and grain and food ships. Last year I urged that our merchant marine ships should not be sold but should be placed under the control of the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the wheat board, so that this grain could be earned across to Great Britain and stored there instead of in the elevators along the great lakes. I do not want to delay the house any longer. Speaking as a private member I should like to see it conclude its business to-morrow night because I think we have been here long enough. I should like, however, to elaborate on what the British
Canadian Wheat Board

Minister of War said yesterday and quote from the National Review of April, 1939, with reference to the great menace of the submarine to our grain and food trade. I quote:
One apologises for introducing these figures: but memories are short. The great war is almost forgotten, and our younger generation never _ knew it. The unrestricted submarine campaign of 1917-18, however, was the gravest peril that has ever threatened the British empire. It was calculated to break Britain's resistance by the autumn of 1917. If 600,000 tons of shipping were destroyed a month, and about 1,200,000 tons of neutral shipping were scared off through terrorism, the argument ran, tshe war would be won for Germany in five months. It nearly was.
Food was short in England, and severely rationed. Our total imports during the war were reduced by over 19 million tons, roughly 35J per cent, and of this decrease about one-third represented food. There was undoubtedly much hardship, and the more irritation. The general shortage of meat, sugar, and butter, the bad quality of much of the meat and bacon released for civilian consumption, the unaccustomed restrictions on diet and habits, and the increase in the cost of living to about 140 per cent above the figure for 1914, all had their repercussions in the widespread industrial unrest after the war.
And again:
In December, 1916, 167 British and allied ships of 276,400 tons were sunk by UJboats. In January, 1917, the corresponding figures were 180 ships of 285,007 tons; in February, 260 vessels of 469,000 tons: in March, 338 ships hr 524,000 tons; in April, 430 vessels of 852,000 tons. The unrestricted submarine campaign started in February; but April was the worst month of the war. On April 19, 1917, the worst day of this blackest month, eleven British merchantmen and eight fishing craft were sent to the bottom. One out of every four merchant ships that left this country during that terrible month never returned. In all, during the war. 5.408 British, allied and neutral vessels of
11.189,000	tons were sunk by U-boats. The British share of this prodigious total was 2,098 merchant vessels and 578 fishing craft of nearly seven million tons gross.
My point is that the wheat board with a free hand is the only board that should be handling all these problems, and not a government department. I am surprised that the Minister of Agriculture has not done this because he is supposed to be an astute politician. Although I do not agree with him, he is a hard-working minister. I have no quarrel with him; far from it. I believe he is a hard working young minister, but I regret that he did not do something a year ago along the line of my suggestion that he should build storage elevators in Great Britain, and that he take the wheat board into his confidence far more than he was doing, like Mr. Bennett and John I. McFarland did, and I suggested that he should try to get together with the motherland. There are great perils for this country at the present
rMr. Church.]
time. We have a great industry upon which the whole credit of the country depends-the stability of our banks and financial institutions, the traffic of our railways, and the general welfare of Canada. It is not a north and south industry but an east and west industry to the markets of the world. As I said in this house on July 4, 1935, on the second reading of the grain bill of that year:
The best friend of the western wheat grower is the policy of protection, as that policy has been and should be extended and administered by the founders and soldiers of the national policy, the Conservative party of Canada. The western wheat grower has eaten the sour grapes of free _ trade. . No wonder the western wheat growers teeth are set on edge. The western wheat grower has taught himself to believe, or has allowed so-called leaders to persuade him, that wheat growing in western Canada is a continental industry, an industry that must prosper by reason of the admission of the product to the United States market or perish because of its exclusion. I submit that wheat growing in western Canada is the most truly national, the most widely imperial of all Canada's great industries. The markets of the British Empire mean more and the markets of the American section of the North American continent mean less to the wheat growers of Canada than to any other class of Canadian producers.
That has been proven to be true. Here we are to-day, after hon. gentlemen opposite had said they were in favour of the policies of free trade, finding that they have veered round to protection, and of course, properly so. They have adopted all these protective measures of subventions, bonuses, subsidies, crop insurance and all the rest of it.
The premises upon which this bill is based may be here to-day and gone to-morrow in view of the international situation and the emergency of foreign affairs, and we may not be able, unless proper steps are taken now, to give the old country what we have always given her, and always to the great credit of the grain industry of Canada. I believe the minister should confer with the British authorities and see if something cannot be done because the fate of the British empire depends upon food and grain from this great dominion to supply the mother country in peace and war alike. There are two thousand fewer merchant ships to carry our food and wheat, across to the mother country unconvoyed, because the north American squadron has been transferred to home waters and the Mediterranean. We had only 120 convoy ships for the Atlantic in the last war, when there was no wheat board. To-day Great Britain has to protect the seven seas with Japan and Italy against us. Japan and Italy could menace our communications on the seven seas and with their modem type of submarines could sink the ships carrying our

Canadian Wheat Board
grain and other food supplies. Japanese submarines can cross the Pacific and get back to their base without refueling. Italian submarines operating in the Atlantic could sink our ships and get back to their base without refueling. They could even go round the Cape of Good Hope and on towards India and get back to their base without refueling.
We would have hardly any carry-over of wheat to-day if we had done as Australia has done-stored a huge part of the surplus in Britain, built huge grain storage spaces, and also created reservoirs over there to take care of the exportable surplus.
I believe the Minister of Trade and Commerce is the minister to handle the marketing and sale of our grain. It is not a matter for the Minister of Agriculture. Trade and commerce is federal and not a field where you have federal and provincial ministers of agriculture operating. I believe great economies could be effected if the Minister of Trade and Commerce were in charge of the marketing and sale of our grain.
There are so many agricultural bills before the house that it is pretty hard to keep track of them.
In conclusion. I believe that the powers of the wheat board should be enlarged not contracted, especially since 80 per cent of our crop could be utilized in the domestic market. We should have, as in 1935, an advisory body of producers with them. If things are in such a terrible state in this country, with one million people on relief, why has not the wheat board been enlarged, with wider powers conferred upon it to deal with wheat for domestic consumption along the lines I suggested in this house on May 4 of last week? Why would it not be a good idea for the government to authorize definite steps along these lines:
1.	Buy directly 'from the farmer the wheat and corn needed for the domestic market at an adequate price, giving each farmer his proportion based on what he has been producing in recent years.
2.	Close the grain exchanges and forbid all speculation in the necessities of life.
3.	Require millers, cotton manufacturers and other processors to buy what they need from the government.
4.	Permit the farmer who desires to produce more than his quota to sell his surplus in any market outside Canada.
I think the government were badly advised when they did not accept the proposal of Hon. Henry Wallace, secretary of Agriculture in the United States, when he proposed that the United States and Canada should make a survey and consider a policy of dividing
the vast markets in the importing countries as a temporary measure for the orderly marketing of this continent's grain from the commercial aspects jointly in the markets of the world.

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before expressing my views on Bill No. 63, which is now before the house for second reading, I wish to express my appreciation of the acceptance by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) of some of our suggestions this afternoon. They will make Bill No. 83 of greater benefit to the people it is intended to serve. I think time will show the wisdom of his action and encourage him to go all the way we suggested by fixing crop failure areas on the basis of the value of the yield per acre rather than on the basis of the yield per acre in bushels. Ultimately I think that will come about.
Bill No. 63, when enacted into legislation, will confirm the selling of wheat by a wheat board as a permanent policy in this country. I have no objection to that; in fact, I think it is the right thing to do. If we must accept the principle of operating under a wheat board as a permanent policy rather than as a means of dealing with temporary conditions, why not do so openly and adequately rather than by half measures such as this? A wheat board is now in existence. The price may be fixed by order in council later in the crop season when all the facts are available to enable the board and the government to set a price at the proper level when there is some grain to sell-not before the grain has even begun to sprout. But if parliament must fix the price in the spring, why not fix it at an adequate figure? The price of 70 cents at Fort William is the same as 52 cents at Medicine Hat, and less than that further west. A price of 80 cents for No. 1 northern at Fort William gave us about 62 cents net in 1938, and with low yields even a price of 62 cents net is not nearly sufficient to meet the costs of production. With a ten-cent cut in the price per bushel, which this bill provides for, the problem for the individual farmer becomes just that much greater. It well may break the back of one of Canada's major industries.
I am pleased to see that this bill makes provision also for the eastern farmer. That is one of the bright spots in the bill. In my opinion it is the one bright spot in the bill. What is good for western Canada is good for all of Canada. Eastern producers should be fairly provided for as well as western producers, each according to his needs. This is a good step in the right direction. When the western committee were here, I asked
3S64
Canadian Wheat Board

them what consideration they had given to the eastern farmers' claim to the same consideration for which we in the west were asking, and I -was surprised that up to that time they had not given it very serious attention. Anything we can now say will not change the price proposed in this bill, so that, although the great weight of evidence of all speakers in this debate points to the necessity of a minimum price of 80 cents for 1939 to save the foundation industry of Canada from complete rout, I shall say no more until the bill is in committee.

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext:
When the two bills were before the house the other day, I expressed my opinion very largely on the bill which is now before us. At that time I had intended to say something further, but I found that owing to a few interruptions and so forth my time was cut down and I could not say precisely what I wanted to say about bill 83. But I should like to join with the hon. member (Mr. Mitchell) who has just spoken in saying that, although I was not in the house this afternoon because I was attending the banking and commerce committee, I believe , that some of the amendments which were made this afternoon have improved the bill, and while I regard it as inadequate as a crop insurance plan, I hope it will be the initial step in working out a crop insurance plan which will be on a sounder, better, fairer and juster basis than the bill which was passed this afternoon.
The bill before us, No. 63, is the one which has caused the bitterest opposition in western Canada. Those of us who come from Saskatchewan know of the enormous petitions which were presented to the members individually from their constituencies. I am not going to read the list, although I have it before me. I am just going to say that between us the members from Saskatchewan received petitions which had upon them 155,204 names. That showed an enormous dissatisfaction with what it was proposed to do, and what it is proposed to do under this bill, because 70 cents as an initial price-and that is what it is called-is inadequate to meet the costs of production and do those things which are necessary in order to maintain the agricultural industry.

Every one of those
signatures was in favour of Bill No. 83.

subtopic: POWERS OF BOARD RESPECTING THE MARKETING OF WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT OF 70 CENTS A BUSHEL
speechtext:
Yes. I said that I too approved the principle of Bill No. 83. I think we are all agreed that some form of crop insurance would be beneficial; and as I said, I hoped that this was but the initial step and (Mr. Mitchell.]
that, after experience, we might have something better than the bill which was passed this afternoon. But I am not criticizing the principle of that bill. What I am saying and what I want to say explicitly is, that the two things should be kept entirely separate and distinct, and that in my opinion Bill No. 63 deals with the industry as an industry, and not with the condition as a relief problem, and that upon the basis of the initial price in this bill, which appears likely to be the maximum price unless certain things happen, it will bring disaster to the western producer. I believe that justification for that opinion can be found in the Minister of Agriculture's own statement-I think it was last Friday- when he said that the average farm price during the last thirty years for No. 1 northern had been 95 cents. I quote from memory. A et even at the end of that thirty years of a farm price of 95 cents, which in many parts of the prairie provinces means a Fort William price of SI.15, thousands of western farmers are in a state of poverty. Having produced vast quantities of new wealth, having received on an average on the farm 95 cents a bushel for No. 1 northern in the last thirty years, nevertheless they find themselves to-day in the condition which we have described.
As a result, farmers have been demanding, and I believe they are justified in demanding, an adequate minimum price. The hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Weir) said he did not think that any government of any political stripe in power in the Dominion of Canada would attempt to do better in the way of price than the present government is doing. Well, our little group may be a long way from power, but I want to say this, that a government with a policy and a program almost identical with that which we are advocating in Canada is now in power in our sister dominion of New Zealand, and has set prices of cheese and butter which were arrived at in accordance with the costs of production, after a very careful inquiry. As a matter of fact, I have before me at the moment a book -I am not going to quote from it-written by Mr. John A. Lee, MJ, parliamentary under-secretary to the Minister of Finance of New Zealand, in which he shows that by the first step which the government of New Zealand took, in taking over the central bank of New Zealand and making it an instrument of national policy, and by the utilization of the central bank and the control of exports and of the international currency which came to them, they were able to do something in the way of fixed prices for agriculture. I believe that if our own banking system were used as an instrument of national policy,

Canadian Wheat Board
something of that kind could be done for agriculture and for our other industries. So I say that if a government with a policy of that description were in power in Canada, they could give a more adequate return to the western farmer than is proposed under the present bill.
There are a good many arguments which one could bring in support of a wheat board, and in support of an adequate fixed price, and I believe that SO cents is the irreducible minimum upon which the average farmer in western Canada can operate. Indeed I do not believe that 80 cents is high enough. It represents something of a compromise which the producers thought might be acceptable to the federal government; and now we find an initial price of 70 cents. There are a good many arguments which one could bring in support of that contention, but to-night, doing what I usually do not do, I am going to confine myself to placing before the house the considered opinion of the committee which came to Ottawa in April and submitted reasons why they though the 80 cent price was the one which should be adopted for the current year. I will not read the preamble.
I will confine myself to the facts bearing upon this particular bill:
We submitted to you our considered conclusion that the continuance of a guarantee of not less than 80 cents for No. 1 northern wheat is the fairest and most feasible method available for the 1939 crop by which western agriculture can be partially saved from the national and partially from the international conditions which those" who depend upon wheat-growing had obviously not created and were powerless to control.
In support of our case we advanced arguments which can very briefly be summarized as follows:
(a)	The west, the expansion and development of which made possible the growth of modern Canada, has made a tremendous contribution by way of purchase of goods and the payment of tariffs to the prosperity of eastern Canada and is justified in asking, as a partial return, for national support in its own special emergency as a reciprocal national contribution.
(b)	This request is particularly reasonable and its granting particularly essential at the present time, because of the ever present necessity of selling some two-thirds of our output in international markets where we receive no protection for our product.
(c)	The assistance actually rendered to the
wheat industry over a period of years had been infinitesimal in relation to its contribution to the production of national wealth.	_
(d)	The same economic disaster which threatened our wheat growers in 1938 is still as near in 1939 unless the government is prepared to continue the same measure of justified support.
(e)	An 80 cent wheat price which means an estimated average price of 57 cents on the western farm does not bring prosperity, but in the main only a restricted level of almost bare subsistence. It is not more than equivalent to
the unsupported domestic price obtained by eastern farmers for similar grains.
(f)	A determined national effort to meet the western emergency is also necessary to maintain a satisfactory national credit position which would be seriously jeopardized by a breakdown in the financial structure of western Canada inevitably resultant from an abandonment of western agriculture to the prevailing disastrously low wheat prices.
(g)	The wheat industry should not be expected to bear the impossible simultaneous double burden of high tariff and other costs and low wheat prices.
(h)	Any disturbance of the balance of western agriculture with its natural concentration upon wheat growing must be also a devastating disturbance of eastern agriculture. It is in the national interest to prevent a disorderly retreat from wheat.
(i)	The wheat board plan cipupled with
adequate price protection, in spite of some inequalities which are at least no less inevitable in any alternative plan, is the simplest _ and most effective method of tiding over in a period of emergency a temporarily depressed industry.	-
As this is a brief and perhaps inadequate summary of arguments previously advanced, we respectfully refer you to the details _ of our previous submission for their elaboration. To the arguments there presented we now submit some additional matters for your consideration. In doing so we note with satisfaction that the government has by the language of section 3 of its proposed Bill No. 83 _ (an act to assist prairie agriculture) recognized the fact that 1939 can properly be termed an emergency year, by which is presumably meant a year of continuing distress and trial for the western farmer.
May we respectfully draw your attention, Mr. Prime Minister, and hon. gentlemen, to the following facts and arguments:
1.	Barter agreements. Recently completed barter trade agreements under which Argentina and other countries dispose of a substantial volume of wheat in return for goods from other countries have provided a form of competition exceedingly difficult to meet.
2.	Subsidized sales. A recent report shows that the Federal Surplus Commodities Corporation in .the United States has disposed of 68,000,000 bushels of wheat during the present season under its subsidy program. The 'bulk of the subsidized wheat is reported as sold to the United Kingdom. This is a form of competition which it is unfair to expect the wheat growers to meet without a reasonable measure of price assistance.
May I interject that the way in which this subsidy is being paid in the United States is by assigning some 30 per cent of the tariff revenue collected for the agricultural industry. In other words, in that country it is recognized that agriculture is entitled to a compensating adjustment by reason of tariff protected industries.
3.	Agriculture is entitled to as much consideration in the shaping of national policies and trade agreements as are our secondary industries. It is not necessary to emphasize the fact that national trade, fiscal, monetary and tariff policies have hitherto functioned

Canadian Wheat Board
primarily in the interests of the development of our secondary industries and against the best interests of agriculture.

I do not think this has been drawn to the attention of the house at all. I can read what remains in five minutes.
The western conference, as has already been indicated, was summoned to face facts, however unpleasant. We derive some comfort from the hope that the present situation is not permanent. Our belief is that any improvement in international relations and economic conditions in Europe will bring about a better balance between production and consumption, and must be reflected in an improvement in wheat prices.
In repeating our prior request for an 80 cent guarantee and before proceeding to analyze the published alternative proposals of the government, may we in conclusion of this portion of our submission respectfully affirm the following:
. 1- Western Canada is practically unanimous m supporting our application for a continuation of the present price protection as a minimum requirement to maintain economic stability in the west during the coming year.
They went on to say that various individual members of this delegation support this statement.
2.	The organized producers of eastern Canada, knowing the special needs of western agriculture and fearful of the effects of the disorganization of the Canadian agricultural economy which would inevitably follow if reasonable wheat prices are not maintained, have, we are advised, already indicated to the government their general support of our position.
3.	Representatives of industry and finance recognize their own partial dependence upon the western farmer, and are not in the main opposed to a continuance of national assistance to the wheat industry, but in general support it as a necessary national safeguarding of the national interest.
We now ask your permission to deal briefly with the proposed legislative program of the government in so far as it affects western agriculture.
Then they go on to discuss the other bill.
I do not propose to put that upon the record because I am dealing at the moment with Bill No. 63. But I wanted to place upon the record the considered opinion of the group representing many western interests, arrived at in connection with Bill No. 63. In my

Electoral Matters-Special Committee
opinion, the western prairies-and I speak not of the farmers only but of the people generally who live there-face disaster it the initial price of 70 cents should prove to be the maximum price during the coming year. The agricultural industry cannot operate on that low return, and after years of low prices the farmers were hoping that they might be able to replenish some of their depleted household necessities, clothing and so on.
So far as the limitation of 5,000 bushels is concerned, I agree with what the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) said earlier this evening, and would merely add that again and again in this house in these debates the cost of production of highly mechanized industry on large farms has been quoted as the basis. If we are to compete in a world in which there is to be keen competition, it seems to me that instead of fewer highly efficient mechanized farms producing a commodity for the world market we shall have more large mechanized farms producing for that market. The only alternative is that the people engaged in the production of these commodities shall accept, as I said the other day, a peasant level of subsistence-and I mean "peasant ' not in the sense in which it was perhaps taken the other day, but in the sense of the low standard of living of the land workers that is to be found in the European countries. So, if we are going to limit the delivery of wheat, we should also take into consideration this fact, that the men who over the last ten years have been tilling a section or more of land have, because of the conditions, each year sustained proportionately heavier losses than those who have been operating smaller farms in the same districts, and they ought to be entitled to some consideration. I recognize, of course, that it may be necessary to take delivery on a graduated scale up to so many hundreds or thousands of bushels at one price and, above that, at a perhaps lower price; nevertheless to throw a large quantity of non-board wheat into the open market in competition with board wheat may have a bad effect not only upon the farmers themselves but upon the experience of the government in handling this wheat through its board.
On motion of Mr. Blaekmore, the debate was adjourned.

speechtext: I should like to debate this bill. Could this motion not be made to-morrow? I am expecting a report on this bill. It is rather an important one.

subtopic: PRESCOTT AND OGDENSBURG BRIDGE COMPANY
speechtext: This is the first instance of this kind since the motion was passed suspending the rules of the house a few days ago. Bills from the senate when reported here are supposed to be read the first time. This bill will stand for second reading; proposing it to-night will give the hon. member a chance to have the bill referred to the committee on private bills.

subtopic: PRESCOTT AND OGDENSBURG BRIDGE COMPANY

I suggest that it should go not to the private bills committee but to the committee on railways, where such bills have always been sent. This is rather an important bill. I think it should have a little more consideration than it is being given.
